Copier en Markdown Avancé On 10 November 2026 Google DeepMind published AlphaProof Code and a companion paper claiming something that has never been claimed before: the first proofs of protocol-level security properties for a widely deployed, unmodified implementation of a cryptographic protocol. The target was Signal. The output was roughly 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean. It hit 643 points and 185 comments on Hacker News the same day. The thread's top-voted objection was a good one: they verified a library with a bug history and found zero bugs? That reads like a red flag, and the usual follow-up — "they must have proved something narrow" — is partly right and mostly beside the point. This page is the practitioner read. Not "AI can prove code correct now," which is false, and not "it's all hype," which is also false. The interesting content is in the trust arithmetic: what is actually machine-checked, what is assumed, and which part of this a team outside DeepMind can copy today. What you'll learn Avoid the naming trap: AlphaProof Code shares a brand with 2024's AlphaProof and almost nothing of its architecture — no reinforcement learning, no tree search Understand why proving things about an ELF binary instead of Rust source puts the Rust compiler OUTSIDE the trusted base — and what that buys and costs Do the trust arithmetic: 6.5M lines of untrusted proof resting on ~26,000 lines of specification that a human has to read and believe Know why zero bugs were found, why that was never the goal, and what the two reinjected bugs actually tested Steal the anti-cheating architecture — the held-out spec directory, the critic that never sees a proof attempt, and the amendment protocol — which is the transferable engineering idea Read the scope table honestly: no constant-time claim, no concurrency, no group messaging, no keygen, and not Signal's shipped apps Apply a six-step protocol to the next 'AI verified our code' announcement
documents.s: AI Formal Verification: 6.5M Lines of Proof on 26,000 Lines of Trust

documents.t: A team of five humans, directing 40–80 agents powered by Gemini 4 Carbon on a single machine over four weeks, produced two independent machine-checked security proofs — one symbolic, one computational — about the AArch64 binary of a purpose-built CLI harness around libsignal-protocol v0.105.4's one-to-one session path, resting on about 26,000 lines of trusted specification and machine semantics, with the Lean kernel as the only thing that has to be right for the proofs themselves. Every clause in that sentence is doing work. Here is why.

The 2024 AlphaProof was a reinforcement-learning system: a language model coupled to AlphaZero, training itself on Lean proofs, which got 28/42 at IMO 2024 (silver-medal level, solving 4 of 6 problems) and published its methodology in Nature in November 2025. AlphaProof Code has none of that machinery. No AlphaZero loop, no RL, no proof-search tree is described anywhere in the paper. It is a multi-agent framework in which "general-purpose coding agents whose behavior is defined by skills: natural-language documents" write Lean, and Lean's kernel checks it. The agents are ordinary LLM agents with role prompts. The reliability comes from the checker, not the prover. What you'll learn Two systems, one brand, different architectures. If you cite "AlphaProof" as evidence that RL-trained provers now verify production code, you have merged two unrelated results. Nothing in the 2026 paper claims the 2024 system is a component. That distinction matters for forecasting. A scaling story about self-play does not transfer here. What transfers is a story about agent orchestration against a sound checker — which is a much more copyable thing, and the reason this page exists.
documents.s: 1. This is not the AlphaProof you remember

documents.t: Most verification work proves things about source code, which means you then have to trust the compiler — hence CompCert, hence years of work. AlphaProof Code went the other way. The unmodified Rust crates are compiled by stock rustc to an AArch64 Linux ELF, and the theorems are about that binary, interpreted by a formal semantics of AArch64 written in Lean covering 467 instructions and 31 system calls in 7,578 lines. The consequence is stated flatly in the paper's trusted-base discussion: "The Rust compiler is not trusted." You do not need to believe rustc is correct, because you never reason about Rust. The price is equally sharp, and an HN commenter put it better than most coverage did: the guarantee attaches to that ELF. Change a compiler flag, bump rustc, relink — and you have a different binary that the theorem says nothing about. The reproduction instructions pin rustc 1.98.1 and warn not to override it, because the generated Lean depends on exact compiler output. Two further limits live in the semantics itself. It does not model threads, signals, the vDSO, dynamic linking, or files outside the working directory — so this is a single-threaded, statically linked process, and nothing about concurrency is proven. And soundness of the semantics cannot be proved, since hardware and kernels are not formal objects; it is validated by differential testing against Unicorn, ARM's Sail Armv9.4-A model, and qemu-aarch64.
documents.s: 2. The proof is about a binary, and that is the clever part

documents.t: No new defect in libsignal was found or reported. That is not a hidden failure; it is a category error in how the result was read. What DeepMind did instead was mutation testing of the specification. Two real, previously fixed libsignal bugs were reintroduced into an isolated copy, and the system produced machine-checked proofs that the buggy versions were insecure: Reinjected bug What went wrong Upstream fix commit weak state A prekey message that decrypted only under an archived session still caused libsignal to store the new session state — including a copy of the signed prekey's secret cd361186fba60c83186262d91b03af608fb8c7c3 small subgroup The PQXDH responder did not check that the initiator's X25519 base key was torsion-free and in range, so a replayed handshake with a mangled base key creates a second session sharing the same secret 5293caa6cad81566b80f3c3731857bedaa78737b Both bugs were discovered by prior human research (Cheval et al., 2026), not by AlphaProof Code. Their role here is to answer the only question that makes a specification credible: would this spec have caught a real bug? Watch out The repo is more careful than the blog post. Per the project's own PAPER_MAP.md, the four symbolic mutant disproofs are proved against an earlier statement, and retargeting them to the final headline theorem is pending (tracked as T-12(d)); the computational disproofs live on unmerged branches; ten synthetic bug-injection obligations remain sorry-exempt stubs on main; and the mutant disproofs get no comparator replay against a held-out challenge. If you repeat the blog's "in both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure," repeat this caveat with it. That gap between a blog's summary and a repo's issue tracker is the single most reusable habit from this page: the artifacts were published, so the caveats are checkable. Most AI-verification announcements do not give you that.
documents.s: 3. Zero bugs were found — because it was never a bug hunt

documents.t: Here is the shape of the result, from the paper's own counts: Layer Size Who has to be right Proofs (untrusted) ~6.5M lines of Lean — 5.3M about the binary (shared by both proofs), ~860k computational, ~350k symbolic Nobody. The Lean kernel checks them Reinjected-bug proofs ~140,000 lines Nobody Allocator proofs ~70,000 lines Nobody Specification directories ~54,000 lines total — Trusted spec you must read ~18,000 lines in the repo + ~8,000 lines of AArch64 semantics ≈ 26,000 You Verified code ~560 KB, ~140,000 AArch64 instructions — The 6.5 million is the number that travelled, and it is the least important one. Proofs are untrusted by construction: the gatekeeper requires that Lean's kernel accept them and that only Lean's three standard axioms are used — propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice. A wrong proof does not typecheck. The 26,000 is the number that decides whether the result means anything, because a specification "must be trusted … and it cannot be automatically checked—a flaw could weaken the guarantee the theorem provides." This is the specification gap, and the paper is unusually candid about it, listing five mitigations: skeptical reviewer agents, machine-checked satisfiability and vacuity theorems, mutation testing, historical-bug disproofs, and human review — while conceding that "human review is not expected to detect all bugs in a large codebase." Note the two 140,000s in that table are different units: 140,000 lines of Lean for the bug proofs, and 140,000 AArch64 instructions of verified code. They are unrelated. One detail worth knowing, because it is the kind of thing that never makes a press release: the specifications themselves were "developed through an intense back-and-forth between humans and agents powered by Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5." The proofs were produced entirely by Gemini 4 Carbon teams. And "none of the authors wrote any proof code."
documents.s: 4. The trust arithmetic: 6.5 million lines resting on 26,000

documents.t: The obvious attack on any AI verification system is: the agent will just weaken the spec until the code verifies. Hacker News raised exactly this. The paper's design is a direct, mechanical answer, and it is the part a team outside DeepMind can copy this week — in Lean, in a property-test suite, or in a CI gate. Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Separate the roles so no agent can both write and bless⌄ Seven roles with disjoint powers: an orchestrator that schedules but never edits Lean, proof workers, a team lead for context management, an architect that decomposes proofs, an integrator that is the only role allowed to commit, a critic, and a gatekeeper. The division is the control, not a convenience. ←PreviousNext→ 2Put the specification where no prover can reach it⌄ The spec is copied into a held-out directory that no agent can write to. Provers work against their own copy and can never silently edit the thing they are being measured against. ←PreviousNext→ 3Diff the spec mechanically before accepting any proof⌄ A tool called comparator must confirm that the headline theorem statement AND every definition it transitively depends on are byte-identical to the held-out copy — not merely that a theorem with that name typechecks. This is the step that closes the 'agent edited the goalpost' hole. ←PreviousNext→ 4Allow amendments, but make them expensive and adversarial⌄ Provers cannot edit the spec; they may propose an amendment to a critic. The critic requires demonstrated necessity (a machine-checked disproof or a concrete counterexample), no weakening of any security property, and a small diff. A real accepted example: memcpy may copy from read-only memory. ←PreviousNext→ 5Keep the critic blind to the proof attempts⌄ The critic approves amendments and never sees proof attempts. It cannot be argued into relaxing a property because a particular proof is almost working — the most natural way such a review gets captured. ←PreviousNext→ 6Anchor on a checker you did not write, with an enumerated axiom list⌄ Lean's kernel is the trust anchor, and the gate asserts that only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice were used. An agent cannot smuggle in an axiom that makes the goal trivial. ←PreviousNext→ 7Publish the artifacts so the caveats are auditable⌄ The Lean proofs, specs, build pins and a paper-to-repo map are public. This is why the gaps in section 3 above are knowable at all — and it is the standard to hold the next announcement to. ←PreviousNext→ What you'll learn Generalise step 3 and you have a rule that applies far outside Lean: a passing check is only evidence if the checked property is byte-identical to one you wrote and stored out of reach. The same failure mode is why agents edit tests instead of code — see Reward hacking in coding agents.

The scope is far narrower than "Signal is now verified." Two independent proofs were produced about the libsignal-cli harness covering only init (process_prekey_bundle), send (message_encrypt) and recv (message_decrypt). Proven — symbolic (Dolev–Yao) model. Ten theorems holding on every collision-free execution: forward secrecy, post-compromise security of message keys, handshake authentication, KCI resistance, handshake secrecy including against an attacker who later breaks Diffie–Hellman, session independence, and "no run faults or diverges." Proven — computational model. Confidentiality and authenticity with forward secrecy and post-compromise security for PQXDH composed with the Triple Ratchet, stated as a concrete bound on the attacker's advantage. Because the normal-termination requirement rules out faulting runs, memory-safety-style faults are excluded as a side effect — writes to executable memory, unmapped access, permission violations — for the modelled runs only. Now the other column, which is longer: Not covered Detail Constant-time / side channels No timing, cache or power-analysis claim appears anywhere. Do not let anyone imply one Concurrency The semantics models no threads and no signals The rest of libsignal poksho, zkgroup, zkcredential, signal-crypto, attest, usernames, media are entirely out of scope Key generation keygen is unverified Group messaging Future work. More than two parties is explicitly out The primitives themselves Specified by contracts, not proven — 37 external hooks plus 18 panic externs. If a real routine does not honour its modelled contract, the guarantee does not hold Signal's shipped apps The result is about their build of libsignal-cli run as a fresh process. Extending to Android or iOS is conditional on trusting those environments preserve the code's behaviour Quantum attackers, multi-device state Named in the paper's own "not covered" row, along with SPQR's post-quantum healing and adversarial first messages to later-promoted sessions And the limit that deserves its own paragraph: the computational bound goes vacuous at scale. If nearly every message starts a new epoch, the statistical terms make the bound vacuous for single sessions of about 25,000 messages, or for 2^20 sessions of 2^10 messages. Keep the conditional clause attached — the threshold only bites under that near-every-message assumption, and quoting the number bare overstates it. The symbolic proof also carries hard input caps baked into the statements: stdin at most 2^20 bytes, send plaintext at most 10^6 bytes, exactly two provisioned honest parties with fixed roles, one active session per file, canonical protobuf encoding only, and 1 GiB of modelled physical memory.
documents.s: 6. What was proven, and what was not

documents.t: Verified: libsignal-protocol v0.105.4 (released 22 October 2026) with spqr v1.6.0. Shipped since: v0.106.0, v0.106.1, v0.106.2 and v0.107.0 — and v0.107.0 landed on 10 November 2026, the same day as the announcement. v0.106.0 changed session management from Sesame to Tahini and cut archived sessions from 40 to 3, which is exactly the area the "weak state" bug lived in. What you'll learn This is the structural cost of binary-level verification, not a scheduling slip. The proof is pinned to one compiled artifact; the library it describes moves on its own release cadence. Any "our code is formally verified" claim needs a version number next to it, and a story for what happens at the next release.
documents.s: 7. It was already stale on announcement day

documents.t: Measure AlphaProof Code For comparison Human team 5 people, 4 weeks (proof work) seL4: ~20 person-years. CompCert: ~6 Proof code written by authors None — Agents per campaign 40–80, on a single machine, 24–72 hours — Compute cost Not reported anywhere — no GPU/TPU hours, no token counts, no dollars — Human review targeting Agents flagged "just one percent of the codebase" for a second human look — blog-only claim, not restated in the paper — Clean proof rebuild Several hours, 15–34 GiB peak RAM — The seL4 comparison is the honest headline. Even taking every number at face value, an HN commenter's arithmetic stands: a 10x productivity gain still leaves Linux-scale verification needing decades or very large expert teams. What changed is not that verification became cheap — it is that a four-week, five-person budget now reaches a target that previously needed a multi-year research programme.
documents.s: 8. The numbers that actually reframe things

documents.t: You cannot run AlphaProof Code — there is no product, API, preview, waitlist or pricing. What you can do is re-check the proofs, which is a genuinely useful exercise if you are evaluating this class of claim. The artifacts are at google-deepmind/code-verification (Apache-2.0 for Google's code; third_party/libsignal/ remains AGPL-3.0-only). Re-check the published Lean proofs (Linux, several hours, 15–34 GiB RAM) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Toolchain pins are exact — the generated Lean depends on precise rustc output # Lean 4 via elan, pinned to leanprover/lean4:v4.34.0 # Rust 1.98.1 exactly, targets aarch64-unknown-linux-{gnu,musl} # plus protoc, LLVM ld.lld 22.1.8, Zig 0.16.0 git clone https://github.com/google-deepmind/code-verification cd code-verification lake exe cache get ulimit -S -s 524288 LAKE_RESTORE_ARTIFACTS=true lake build # Rebuild the verified binary from stock rustc and confirm it matches the pin ./scripts/cli-elf-stock --stdbin --build ./scripts/cli-elf-stock --verify-pin lake build CliElfLib lake script run checkCliElfOwner # Tune threads to RAM: roughly one thread per 4 GiB free # export LEAN_NUM_THREADS=4 The comparator replay tool is Linux-only — it sandboxes builds with landrun/Landlock. And the thing actually worth reading is not the 6.5M lines; it is the ~18,000 lines of trusted specification, because that is the part no machine checked for you. The transferable half is the review discipline. You can run the same adversarial shape against a specification in any language: Adversarial specification review — run this against your own spec, tests or acceptance criteria CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are a skeptical reviewer. Here is a specification that a system claims to satisfy. Your job is NOT to confirm it. Your job is to find the gap between what it states and what a reader will believe it states. <specification> {paste the spec, property test, or acceptance criteria} </specification> Answer in five numbered sections, concretely and with no hedging: 1. VACUITY. Is there a trivial model that satisfies every clause? Describe a system that passes this spec and is obviously useless or insecure. 2. SCOPE. List every behaviour a reader would ASSUME is covered that is not actually stated. Be specific about concurrency, failure paths, resource limits and timing. 3. ASSUMPTIONS. Enumerate what is assumed rather than established, including anything hooked, mocked, stubbed or specified by contract instead of verified. 4. MUTATION TEST. Propose three concrete bugs that this spec would NOT reject. For each, say exactly which clause fails to bite and why. 5. SCALE. Identify any bound, budget or quantifier that becomes vacuous or unenforceable as inputs, sessions or message counts grow. Give the threshold. Do not suggest improvements. Report only what is missing or unenforceable.

There will be more of these, and most will be weaker. Six questions, in order of how much they tell you: What is in the trusted base, and how many lines is it? If nobody publishes this number, there is no result to evaluate. "6.5 million lines of proof" is marketing; "26,000 lines you must read" is the claim. What exactly was the subject? A binary, a source tree, a module, a function? Which version? Pin it against the project's current release — if the verified version is several releases behind, say so. What properties, stated as theorems? "Secure" is not a property. Forward secrecy, KCI resistance and normal termination are. Demand the "not covered" column, and check specifically for constant-time, concurrency and multi-party claims, which are the three most often silently absent. Was the specification tested, not just satisfied? Look for mutation testing, vacuity and satisfiability theorems, and historical-bug disproofs. A spec nothing can fail is a spec that proves nothing. Could the prover touch the specification? If there is no held-out copy and no mechanical diff of the statement and its dependencies, assume the goalpost moved. Are the artifacts public and the caveats auditable? This result's real weaknesses — the pending retarget, the unmerged branches, the sorry stubs — are knowable only because the repo shipped. Treat an unpublished proof as an unverified claim. Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways AlphaProof Code shares a name with 2024's AlphaProof and almost nothing else: no RL, no AlphaZero, no tree search. It is LLM agents writing Lean against a sound kernel — a far more copyable design than self-play. The headline number is the wrong one. 6.5M lines of proof are untrusted by construction; ~26,000 lines of specification are what a human must read and believe. Ask for that number first, every time. Proving things about the ELF binary keeps rustc out of the trusted base — and pins the guarantee to one build. The verified version, v0.105.4, was already four releases behind on announcement day. Scope is much narrower than 'Signal is verified': one-to-one init/send/recv only, primitives hooked by contract, no constant-time claim, no concurrency, no groups, no keygen, not the shipped apps. The computational bound goes vacuous at roughly 25,000 messages in a single session when nearly every message starts a new epoch. Quote the threshold with its condition attached. Steal the architecture, not the headline: a held-out spec directory, a comparator that diffs the statement and all its dependencies, a blind critic for amendments, and an enumerated axiom allowlist. That pattern generalises to any check an agent could otherwise edit. Five people, four weeks, 40–80 agents on one machine, and none of the authors wrote proof code — against seL4's ~20 person-years. Verification did not become cheap; it became reachable on a sprint budget. Dernière vérification : 2026-11-11. Line counts, team size, the four-week figure, the model attributions, the vacuity threshold and the trusted-base discussion are from the paper's HTML edition. Scope and property lists are from its Table 1 and limitations sections. Toolchain pins, axiom allowlist, build timings and the pending-retarget caveats are from the artifacts repo and its docs/PAPER_MAP.md. The "one percent of the codebase" human-review figure appears in the DeepMind blog post only and is not restated in the paper — treat it as a blog claim. Versions move: libsignal v0.107.0 shipped 10 November 2026, so the verified v0.105.4 falls further behind over time. The framework itself is not available to use; if that changes, this page is stale. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.

documents.t: Introducing AlphaProof Code — Google DeepMind — the announcement: the four-week framing, "powered by Gemini Carbon", the reinjected-bug claim, the one-percent human-review figure, and the forward look toward medical-device firmware and grid software AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal's Security at the Machine-Code Level — the paper in full HTML. Source for the four components, the seven agent roles, the 40–80 agents / 24–72 hours figure, the line-count breakdown, Table 1's covered/not-covered split, the AArch64 semantics scope (467 instructions, 31 syscalls, 7,578 lines), the trusted-base discussion including "the Rust compiler is not trusted", and the vacuity threshold PDF edition of the paper — same content, citable form google-deepmind/code-verification — the Lean artifacts: Computational/, Symbolic/, LibsignalBinary/, arm64-semantics/, comparator/. Apache-2.0 with third_party/libsignal/ AGPL-3.0-only; "not an official Google product"; in scope for Google's OSS VRP docs/PAPER_MAP.md — the paper-to-repo map, and the most honest document in the set: the 37 hooks and 18 panic externs, the T-12(d) pending retarget, the conditional ROM corollary, and the symbolic model's hard input caps Symbolic/BugInjection/README.md — the two reinjected bugs with their upstream fix commits signalapp/libsignal — the real library and its crate list, which is how you see that only libsignal-protocol plus spqr were in scope. Releases confirm v0.105.4 (22 Oct 2026) and the v0.106.x / v0.107.0 line that followed leanprover/comparator — the held-out-spec diff tool, sandboxed with Landlock leanprover/lean4 — the kernel that is the actual trust anchor; this work pins v4.34.0 AlphaProof (2024): AI solves IMO problems at silver-medal level — the other AlphaProof: RL plus AlphaZero, 28/42 at IMO 2024, methodology published in Nature in November 2025 Introducing CodeMender — the repair-side agent the blog pairs this with Hacker News discussion, 10 November 2026 — 643 points, 185 comments. The "found zero bugs?" objection, the layered "trust us" critique, the correct observation that the guarantee is bit-for-bit to one binary, and the seL4 scaling arithmetic Related on AILmanac: The Verification Bottleneck · Reward hacking in coding agents · The capability–reliability gap · Reviewing third-party code

The Verification Bottleneck — the constraint this result is aimed at: why trusting code, not writing it, is what limits an AI-heavy team Reward hacking in coding agents — the same failure mode without the gatekeeper: what happens when the agent can edit the thing that grades it Code Erosion — the empirical other end of the spectrum: what agents do to working code when nothing machine-checks the result Partager cette page X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News Copier le lien

Copier en Markdown Avancé Almost every coding benchmark you have read about asks the same question: given a task, can the agent solve it? One prompt, one patch, one verdict. That setup is convenient and it hides the failure mode that actually costs you money, because real software is never written once. The spec moves. You extend what you built last week. And the interesting question is not whether the agent can write the feature — it is what the agent does to the code that was already working. SlopCodeBench exists to measure exactly that, and the results are worse than the discourse suggests. In the paper's own words: "Software development is iterative, yet agentic coding benchmarks hide design issues through their single-shot setup." Two things made it worth a page this week. First, a third-party campaign report — "SlopCodeBench 10/2026 – Opus 5.5, Astra wins overall, xhigh considered harmful" — reached 260 points and 101 comments on Hacker News on 15 October 2026, following a 405-point post on the same benchmark in July. Second, almost nobody is quoting the numbers in it that matter most. The headline travelled; the regression statistic, the cost-per-pass arithmetic and the cleanliness/correctness inversion did not. What you'll learn Explain what SlopCodeBench measures that SWE-bench-style benchmarks structurally cannot — iterative specification refinement, with regression tests carried forward across every checkpoint Read the two pass rates correctly: strict and core rank the same ten campaigns almost in reverse, and which one you quote decides your winner Derive the statistic the reports bury — between 82% and 88% of failing tests at the final checkpoint are regressions, not the new requirement Price effort honestly: every medium campaign beat every xhigh campaign on cost per passing checkpoint, with a 9.7x spread from best to worst Hold two findings together without flinching — Opus 5.5 at xhigh wrote materially cleaner code and passed fewer checkpoints than the same model at medium Apply the paper's most actionable result: telling an agent to write clean code improved its first commit by up to a third and did not change the degradation curve at all Dernière vérification : 2026-10-21. Two separate sources with different authors are used here and should not be blended. The benchmark and its paper-level findings (36 problems, 196 checkpoints, the 77% / 75.5% erosion rates, the 2.3x / 2.0x comparison against 473 real repositories) come from Orlanski et al., arXiv 2603.24755, submitted 25 March 2026 and revised 7 May 2026. The per-model numbers come from HumanLayer's October 2026 campaign report — a later, independent set of runs by a third party, explicitly one run per model-effort setting. Leaderboards and model versions move; re-check both before quoting. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.
documents.s: Code Erosion: Why Your Agent Breaks What It Already Built

documents.t: SlopCodeBench's unit of work is not a task, it is a trajectory. An agent is given a problem, writes a solution, then receives a new requirement and must modify its own existing code. Repeat. The specifications evolve in ways that force architectural decisions while leaving implementation details open, and — this is the mechanism that makes it bite — tests from earlier checkpoints carry forward. To pass a checkpoint you must satisfy the new requirement and keep every previous one working. The scale, per the paper: 36 problems decomposed into 196 checkpoints total, with 15 coding agents evaluated across open and closed model families. Two metrics come out: Strict pass — every test passes, including every regression test from every earlier checkpoint. Core pass — the looser bar, which gives credit for satisfying the current requirement. And the paper names the two degradation modes it tracks. Structural erosion is complexity concentrating — the code curdling into a few overloaded places. Verbosity is redundant code multiplying. These are measured, not vibes.

From the paper: no agent fully solved any problem end-to-end. Not one of the 15, not one of the 36 problems. The best agent reached 14.8% of checkpoints. Structural erosion increased in 77% of trajectories; verbosity in 75.5%. Compared against a corpus of 473 open-source repositories, agent-written code showed 2.3× greater verbosity and 2.0× more erosion. So the baseline claim is not "agents write slightly messier code than humans." It is: across three-quarters of long-horizon trajectories, the code gets structurally worse as the agent works on it, and the end state is roughly twice as eroded as what humans ship.
documents.s: The result that should be the headline

documents.t: HumanLayer ran ten complete campaigns on the pinned v1.0 catalog with the stock just-solve prompt, seed 42, any-case runner pass policy, in Docker with Python 3.12 and uv. One run per model-effort combination. Campaign Strict Strict rate Core rate Est. cost GPT-6 Astra XHigh 32/196 16.33% 69.39% $758.62 GPT-6 SOL Medium 30/196 15.31% 67.86% $245.69 GPT-6 Astra Medium 29/196 14.80% 66.33% $261.05 GPT-6.1 SOL Medium 29/196 14.80% 65.82% $178.51 Opus 5.5 Medium 28/196 14.29% 73.98% $193.47 GPT-5.6 SOL XHigh 28/196 14.29% 70.92% $753.30 Fable 5.1 XHigh 26/196 13.27% 72.45% $1,550.07 GPT-6 SOL XHigh 26/196 13.27% 68.37% $517.32 Opus 5.5 XHigh 25/196 12.76% 71.94% $817.04 GLM 5.3 XHigh 24/196 12.24% 66.33% $365.13 Look at the strict column first. The entire frontier field lands between 12.24% and 16.33%. The spread from best to worst is 8 checkpoints out of 196. Anyone telling you one of these models is decisively better at long-horizon maintenance is reading noise — especially given one run per cell.

This is the part to internalise before you cite any of it. GPT-6 Astra XHigh is 1st on strict (16.33%) and 5th on core (69.39%). Opus 5.5 Medium is 5th on strict (14.29%) and 1st on core (73.98%) — the best core rate in the table. GPT-6.1 SOL Medium is tied 4th on strict (14.80%) and dead last on core (65.82%). Same ten runs, same data, and the podium reshuffles. The two metrics are measuring genuinely different things: core rate says "how often did it do the new thing," strict rate says "how often did it do the new thing without breaking the old things." A model can be good at one and mediocre at the other, and most of these are. If you only ever remember one rule from this page: ask which pass rate a coding-agent number refers to. The gap between 14.29% and 73.98% for one model on one dataset is the whole argument.
documents.s: The ranking flips depending on which metric you quote

documents.t: The report publishes a final-checkpoint table with failed test cases and, separately, how many of those were regression failures. Divide one column by the other and the benchmark's thesis stops being a thesis. Campaign Final failed tests Regressions Regression share Opus 5.5 Medium 2,508 2,206 88.0% GPT-6 SOL Medium 2,831 2,479 87.6% GPT-6.1 SOL Medium 2,757 2,404 87.2% GPT-5.6 SOL XHigh 2,727 2,376 87.1% GPT-6 Astra Medium 1,747 1,516 86.8% Opus 5.5 XHigh 2,446 2,123 86.8% Fable 5.1 XHigh 2,463 2,126 86.3% GLM 5.3 XHigh 2,748 2,311 84.1% GPT-6 SOL XHigh 1,651 1,366 82.7% GPT-6 Astra XHigh 1,435 1,178 82.1% The regression share column is arithmetic on the report's published counts, not a figure it states. Across all ten campaigns it sits between 82.1% and 88.0% — remarkably tight for ten different configurations across four model families. Read that again: when a frontier coding agent fails at the end of a long iterative task, roughly six failures in seven are things that used to work. Only about one in seven is the feature it was actually asked for. Watch out This is the number that should change your harness, not your model choice. A 4-6 percentage-point difference in strict rate between frontier models is within single-run noise. An 85%-ish regression share is a structural property of how agents edit code — and it is the thing your CI, your test retention policy and your review process can actually act on. It also explains why agents feel better than they measure. Ask for a feature, watch it land, ship it. The regression is three checkpoints away and nobody re-ran the old tests.
documents.s: The statistic nobody quotes: it's regressions, not the new feature

documents.t: Now the finding that got the post to the front page. Three models were run at both medium and xhigh effort: Model Strict: Medium → XHigh Core: Medium → XHigh Cost multiplier Opus 5.5 28 → 25 145 → 141 4.22× GPT-6 SOL 30 → 26 133 → 134 2.11× GPT-6 Astra 29 → 32 130 → 136 2.91× Two of three models got worse on strict passes at higher effort, while costing between 2.11× and 4.22× more. In the author's words: "opus 5.5 did BETTER on medium effort than on xhigh." To their considerable credit, they refuse to oversell it. The report states the finding "doesn't prove that more reasoning hurts coding" — only that "higher effort was not a reliable way to buy more strict passes." And the methodology caveat is stated plainly: "I ran each model and effort setting once... These single runs don't isolate effort as the cause." That caveat is real and you should hold onto it. A 3-checkpoint swing out of 196 is well inside the variance you would expect between two runs of the same configuration. The weak claim is what survives: effort is not a dial that reliably buys correctness on long-horizon work. The strong claim — that xhigh actively damages coding — is not established by this data, and the author doesn't make it.

The effort table is noisy. The economics are not, because cost differences here are large enough to dwarf the noise. Dividing estimated cost by strict passes: Campaign Effort $ per strict pass GPT-6.1 SOL Medium Medium $6.16 Opus 5.5 Medium Medium $6.91 GPT-6 SOL Medium Medium $8.19 GPT-6 Astra Medium Medium $9.00 GLM 5.3 XHigh XHigh $15.21 GPT-6 SOL XHigh XHigh $19.90 GPT-6 Astra XHigh XHigh $23.71 GPT-5.6 SOL XHigh XHigh $26.90 Opus 5.5 XHigh XHigh $32.68 Fable 5.1 XHigh XHigh $59.62 That is my arithmetic on the report's published figures, and the pattern is absolute: every medium campaign is cheaper per passing checkpoint than every xhigh campaign. No overlap. The spread from best to worst is 9.7×. The single starkest comparison in the whole dataset: Fable 5.1 at xhigh spent $1,550.07 to pass 26 checkpoints. Opus 5.5 at medium spent $193.47 to pass 28. Eight times the money, for two fewer passes. Pro tip The actionable version: on long-horizon iterative coding, start at medium and make xhigh prove itself on YOUR workload before you pay for it. The defaults already lean this way — Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 default to medium, and medium is the recommended starting effort for agentic coding on Sonnet 5.5. If you do run a comparison, run each configuration more than once. A single campaign at this benchmark's resolution cannot distinguish a 3-checkpoint effort effect from a 3-checkpoint coin flip.
documents.s: Where the evidence gets much stronger: cost per pass

documents.t: Here is the result that is genuinely hard to explain away, and the most interesting thing in the report. Opus 5.5 at xhigh passed fewer strict checkpoints than Opus 5.5 at medium — and wrote distinctly better code by the slop metrics. Across 28 matched problems, slop coverage was 77.75% for xhigh against 94.25% for medium (92.90% after filtering); the author characterises xhigh's output as "close to ~5x cleaner." A note on that figure, because it matters for how you quote it: ~5× is the author's characterisation of their composite slop metric. It is not derivable from the two coverage percentages above, which differ by about 16 points, not 5×. Cite the coverage numbers if you need something checkable; treat "~5× cleaner" as a directional claim about a metric whose internals you haven't seen. Either way the direction is consistent and the implication is uncomfortable: more reasoning effort bought code that looks better and functions worse. Effort appears to be partly buying architectural taste — refactoring, abstraction, tidiness — and those edits are precisely the ones that break code that already worked. Tidying is a regression risk. A model that leaves the ugly working thing alone scores better on a benchmark that remembers what used to pass. The report's speculation on the gap between pass rates and code metrics is worth repeating: newer models may be generating novel slop patterns that existing linters do not yet detect. Which is a decent reminder that a clean lint report on agent output is evidence about your linter as much as about your code.
documents.s: Cleaner code that works less often

documents.t: One more detail, easy to miss and quietly revealing. Mean cyclomatic complexity across functions and methods: Fable 5.1: 8,967 callables, mean complexity 3.57 GPT-6 SOL Medium: 1,083 callables, mean complexity 11.70 Comparable problems, and an 8.3× difference in how many functions got written. Fable decomposes aggressively into many simple units; GPT-6 SOL writes far fewer, far denser ones. Rank them on mean complexity alone and Fable wins by 3×. Rank them on callable count and the story inverts — all those tiny functions are also where verbosity lives. Neither number means anything alone. This is the general lesson about code-quality metrics on agent output: every single one of them is gameable by an architectural style, so read them in pairs.
documents.s: Two opposite architectural styles, visible in the metrics

documents.t: The paper tested the obvious intervention and the result deserves to be better known: explicit quality guidance reduced initial issues by up to one-third — and did not affect the degradation patterns. Telling the agent to write clean code works, once. It improves the first commit. It does not stop the rot. Erosion is a property of the iterative editing process, not of the agent's initial intent, so instructions aimed at intent don't touch it. Which points the fix somewhere less comfortable than your prompt: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Retain and re-run every old test, every time⌄ An 82-88% regression share is only visible if the old tests still run. If your agent loop validates the current requirement and nothing else, you are measuring core pass rate and shipping strict failures. This is the single highest-leverage change available. ←PreviousNext→ 2Budget review for deletions and refactors, not additions⌄ The cleanliness/correctness inversion says the dangerous edits are the tidy ones. Diffs that reorganise working code deserve more scrutiny than diffs that add new code beside it — the opposite of most review instincts. ←PreviousNext→ 3Start at medium effort and make xhigh earn its multiplier⌄ Every medium campaign beat every xhigh campaign on cost per passing checkpoint, with no overlap. Treat high effort as a hypothesis to test on your own workload, not a quality setting to leave on. ←PreviousNext→ 4Measure erosion over the trajectory, not quality at the end⌄ Track complexity and volume per checkpoint across a long task. A single end-state lint score cannot distinguish code that was always like that from code that got worse every iteration — and the trend is the thing that predicts the next regression. ←PreviousNext→ 5Re-anchor the spec instead of extending the context⌄ Erosion accumulates across checkpoints that each inherit the last one's drift. Periodically restating the full current specification against the current code, rather than appending the next delta, attacks the mechanism directly. ←PreviousNext→ Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways SlopCodeBench measures trajectories, not tasks: the agent extends its own code as the spec evolves, and every earlier test carries forward. No agent has fully solved a single problem end-to-end; the frontier field clusters between 12.24% and 16.33% strict. Strict and core pass rates rank the same ten campaigns almost in reverse. Opus 5.5 Medium is 14.29% strict and 73.98% core. Always ask which one a number refers to. 82-88% of failing tests at the final checkpoint are regressions, not the new requirement — six failures in seven are things that used to work. That is a harness problem, not a model-selection problem. Every medium campaign beat every xhigh campaign on cost per strict pass, with no overlap and a 9.7x spread. Fable 5.1 XHigh: $1,550 for 26 passes; Opus 5.5 Medium: $193 for 28. Effort partly buys tidiness, and tidying working code causes regressions. Opus 5.5 XHigh wrote cleaner code and passed fewer checkpoints — so review refactors harder than additions. Telling the agent to write clean code improved the first commit by up to a third and did nothing to the degradation curve. Erosion lives in the editing process, so fix it with retained tests and per-checkpoint measurement. Read code-quality metrics in pairs: 8,967 callables at mean complexity 3.57 versus 1,083 at 11.70 is two architectural styles, and either metric alone ranks them backwards.
documents.s: What to actually do about it

documents.t: SlopCodeBench: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Degrade Over Long-Horizon Iterative Tasks (arXiv 2603.24755) — Orlanski, Roy, Yun, Shin, Gu, Ge, Adila, Roberts, Sala, Albarghouthi; submitted 25 March 2026, revised 7 May 2026. Source for the benchmark design, 36 problems / 196 checkpoints / 15 agents, the structural-erosion and verbosity definitions, the 77% and 75.5% trajectory rates, the 2.3× / 2.0× comparison against 473 open-source repositories, the "no agent fully solved any problem" result, and the quality-guidance finding. SprocketLab/slop-code-bench — the benchmark implementation (262 stars). Problem catalog, runner and metric code. scbench.ai — leaderboards and the project site. SlopCodeBench 10/2026 — Opus 5.5, Astra wins overall, xhigh considered harmful — HumanLayer's October 2026 campaign report. Source for all ten campaign rows, the medium-vs-xhigh effort table and cost multipliers, the final-checkpoint failure and regression counts, the slop-coverage and complexity figures, the "~5x cleaner" characterisation, the methodology (v1.0 catalog, just-solve prompt, seed 42, any-case policy, Docker/Python 3.12/uv), and the single-run caveat. The cost-per-strict-pass and regression-share columns on this page are my own arithmetic on its published numbers. Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench — the earlier July 2026 report from the same repo (2.8k stars), which reached 405 points on Hacker News. Hacker News discussion, 15 October 2026 — 260 points, 101 comments on the October report. L'ingénierie de prompt porte sur les mots que vous choisissez. L'ingénierie du contexte porte sur l'espace de travail que vous confiez au modèle — ce qu'il contient, dans quel ordre, et ce que vous avez délibérément laissé de côté. La distinction compte parce qu'une fenêtre de contexte n'est pas un bloc-notes. C'est une ressource attentionnelle limitée et coûteuse. La façon dont vous la remplissez change ce sur quoi le modèle se concentre, combien elle vous coûte, et si elle reste utile à mesure que les sessions s'allongent. What you'll learn Distinguer l'ingénierie du contexte de l'ingénierie de prompt — et comprendre pourquoi le domaine a évolué Traiter la fenêtre de contexte comme un budget d'attention, et non comme un espace de stockage Repérer la dégradation du contexte et l'effet perdu au milieu avant qu'ils ne ruinent une longue session Placer les instructions là où l'attention se porte réellement — en haut, à la fin, jamais enfouies au milieu Appliquer les trois tactiques de fond : la compaction, la prise de notes et la récupération juste-à-temps Dernière vérification : 2026-06-29. Anthropic définit l'ingénierie du contexte comme la sélection du "plus petit ensemble possible de tokens à fort signal qui maximisent la probabilité d'un résultat souhaité". Les tactiques et le cadrage ci-dessous suivent ces recommandations officielles — vérifiez-y les détails précis, car les recommandations relatives aux agents évoluent rapidement. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.

Chaque modèle a une taille de contexte maximale — un plafond strict mesuré en tokens. Considérez-le comme un budget. Vous le dépensez en : Votre prompt système et vos instructions permanentes Documents récupérés, extraits de base de code, définitions d'outils Historique de la conversation La sortie du modèle (qui compte elle aussi dans la fenêtre lors des sessions multi-tours) Lorsque vous êtes à court, quelque chose doit céder. Soit l'ancien contenu est supprimé, soit la session se heurte à un mur. La plupart des guides pour débutants traitent la fenêtre de contexte selon le principe « plus, c'est mieux ». L'ingénierie du contexte la traite comme une ressource à allouer avec soin : la dépenser pour ce dont le modèle a réellement besoin pour ce tour, et non pour tout ce qui pourrait être pertinent. Anthropic présente toute cette discipline comme une recherche du « plus petit ensemble possible de tokens à fort signal » — chaque token que vous ajoutez entre en compétition pour un budget d'attention fini, une conséquence directe de la manière dont un transformeur met chaque token en relation avec tous les autres.

Il existe un phénomène bien documenté dans les LLM à long contexte : les modèles accordent une attention disproportionnée au contenu situé près du début et de la fin de leur contexte, tandis que leur rappel du contenu enfoui au milieu se dégrade. Les chercheurs qui ont étudié cet effet l'ont appelé « lost in the middle » (perdu au milieu). La conséquence pratique : si vous remplissez un contexte de 100 000 tokens avec des documents et enfouissez l'instruction la plus cruciale à la position 60 000, le modèle peut l'ignorer de fait — non pas parce qu'il est incapable de lire aussi loin, mais parce que l'attention n'est pas répartie uniformément sur la fenêtre. La « dégradation du contexte » (context rot) désigne le schéma plus large : à mesure qu'une session s'allonge, la qualité des réponses tend à dériver. Les premières instructions se diluent. Les allers-retours répétés évincent la tâche d'origine. Le modèle se met à tergiverser, à se répéter, ou à perdre le fil de ce que vous demandiez réellement. Ce ne sont pas des bugs que vous pouvez entièrement corriger avec un meilleur prompt. Ce sont des propriétés structurelles du fonctionnement de l'attention à grande échelle. La réponse de l'ingénierie consiste à garder le contexte plus petit et plus net, plutôt qu'à le remplir en espérant.
documents.s: La dégradation du contexte et l'effet perdu au milieu

documents.t: L'endroit où vous placez le contenu est aussi important que ce que vous incluez. Bonnes pratiques établies : Position Quoi y mettre Tout en haut (prompt système) Instructions stables et durables. Persona, règles, exigences de format. Après le prompt système La tâche en cours, en termes simples. Juste avant le dernier tour utilisateur Le contexte le plus crucial et spécifique à cette requête précise. Milieu Documents de support, fragments récupérés — ordonnés par pertinence, pas par chronologie. Historique de la conversation Seulement ce qui est nécessaire à la continuité. Élaguez sans hésiter. La règle générale : plus c'est proche du tour en cours, plus cela reçoit d'attention. Les instructions cruciales qui ne vivent qu'au milieu d'un long historique sont en danger.

Un prompt système peut échouer de deux manières opposées. Trop bas, et vous codez en dur une logique fragile de type si-ceci-alors-cela qui se brise dès que la réalité diffère. Trop haut, et vous écrivez des consignes vagues qui supposent un contexte dont le modèle ne dispose pas. Anthropic appelle la cible la « bonne altitude » — la zone idéale qui est « assez spécifique pour guider efficacement le comportement, tout en restant assez flexible pour fournir de solides heuristiques ». Visez là : des règles et des exemples concrets, ni un arbre de décision, ni une impression vague.
documents.s: La « bonne altitude » pour les instructions

documents.t: La tentation est de tout y mettre : tous les documents, l'intégralité de la base de code, toute la conversation. Résistez-y. La meilleure approche est la récupération sélective : identifier ce dont le modèle a réellement besoin pour cette requête précise, et n'injecter que cela. Un fragment de 2 000 tokens bien récupéré du bon document surpasse un déversement de 40 000 tokens où la réponse se trouve quelque part au milieu. C'est pourquoi la génération augmentée par récupération (RAG) existe — non seulement pour dépasser les limites de contexte, mais pour améliorer la qualité en gardant le contexte soigneusement organisé. La version agentique est la récupération juste-à-temps : au lieu de précharger chaque document, l'agent conserve des identifiants légers (chemins de fichiers, ID, requêtes) et n'amène le contenu réel dans le contexte qu'au moment où il en a besoin. Pour les sessions interactives, la même logique s'applique : au lieu de tout accumuler, compactez ou videz périodiquement l'historique pour supprimer le contenu qui n'est plus pertinent pour la tâche en cours. Les commandes /compact et /clear de Claude Code sont des outils d'ingénierie du contexte, pas seulement de gestion de session. Sur l'API, le même schéma est automatisé par l'édition de la mémoire et du contexte — les anciens résultats d'outils sont élagués de la fenêtre tandis que ce qui compte est écrit dans un magasin de mémoire persistant.

Pour le travail à long horizon, trois techniques font l'essentiel du gros œuvre. Elles se composent — la plupart des vrais agents utilisent les trois. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Compaction⌄ Lorsqu'une session approche de la limite de la fenêtre, résumez-la et réinitialisez avec la version distillée. Préservez les détails porteurs — décisions d'architecture, bugs non résolus, choix d'implémentation clés — et abandonnez le déroulé coup par coup. C'est ce que fait /compact dans Claude Code. ←PreviousNext→ 2Prise de notes structurée⌄ Faites en sorte que l'agent écrive des faits durables dans une mémoire externe (un fichier, un bloc-notes, un CLAUDE.md) et les relise plus tard. Cela offre une mémoire persistante avec une surcharge minimale dans la fenêtre — les notes vivent en dehors du budget jusqu'à ce qu'on en ait besoin. ←PreviousNext→ 3Récupération juste-à-temps⌄ Ne préchargez pas tous les documents. Conservez des références légères et chargez le contenu réel à l'exécution, seulement pour l'étape qui en a besoin. Une récupération ciblée de 2 000 tokens bat un déversement de 40 000 tokens. ←PreviousNext→

Les tokens que vous envoyez sont des tokens que vous payez — à la fois en argent et en latence. Remplir le contexte de matériel vaguement pertinent gonfle les deux. L'ingénierie du contexte et l'efficacité des coûts sont le même problème. Plus concrètement : Un prompt système surchargé que vous copiez-collez depuis un modèle est payé à chaque appel. L'ancien historique de conversation que vous traînez parce qu'« il pourrait être utile » est payé à chaque appel. Les documents que vous injectez « au cas où » sont payés à chaque appel. Élaguer ce qui n'a pas besoin d'être là est simultanément meilleur pour la qualité et moins coûteux à exécuter.

Dans Claude.ai : Utilisez des conversations distinctes pour des tâches distinctes. Ne laissez pas un après-midi de digressions polluer le contexte d'un projet ciblé. Résumez les longs fils avant de poser une question complexe qui en dépend. Un résumé explicite est souvent plus utile que l'historique brut. Placez la chose précise que vous voulez à la fin d'un long message, et non enfouie au milieu. Dans Claude Code : Gardez votre fichier CLAUDE.md léger. Chaque ligne qu'il contient est injectée dans chaque session. Voir CLAUDE.md et Gestion du contexte. Utilisez /clear lorsque vous passez à une tâche réellement différente. Utilisez /compact lorsque vous voulez continuer mais que la session grossit. Référencez les fichiers par leur chemin plutôt que de coller leur contenu quand le fichier complet n'est pas nécessaire pour l'étape en cours. Au niveau de l'API : Concevez les prompts système pour ne contenir que ce dont chaque requête a véritablement besoin. Déplacez les instructions spécifiques à la tâche dans le tour utilisateur. Pour les cas d'usage riches en documents, récupérez et injectez les fragments pertinents plutôt que de téléverser un corpus entier. Structurez le prompt de sorte que le préfixe stable et réutilisable vienne en premier — cela active aussi la mise en cache de prompt, un compagnon naturel de l'ingénierie du contexte. Lorsque vous voulez confier un long document à Claude, la règle de placement bat le volume brut à tous les coups : Instruction en premier, redite en dernier CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Tâche : Trouve chaque clause où ce contrat plafonne notre responsabilité, et cite-les toutes mot pour mot avec leur numéro de section. [... coller ici le contrat complet de 40 pages ...] Rappel de la tâche : liste toutes les clauses de plafonnement de responsabilité ci-dessus, citées exactement, avec les numéros de section. S'il n'y en a aucune, dis-le explicitement. La même instruction figure en haut et en bas — les deux positions favorisées par l'attention — afin qu'elle survive même à un très long milieu.
documents.s: Tactiques pratiques pour les utilisateurs de Claude

documents.t: L'ingénierie de prompt demande : « Que devrais-je dire ? » L'ingénierie du contexte demande : « Que devrait voir le modèle, dans quel ordre, et que devrais-je délibérément exclure ? » La seconde question est plus difficile, mais c'est celle qui détermine réellement la qualité à grande échelle. Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways La fenêtre de contexte est un budget d'attention, pas un stockage — dépensez-la uniquement sur des tokens à fort signal. La position bat le volume : les instructions cruciales vont en haut et juste avant le tour final, jamais enfouies au milieu. La compaction, la prise de notes et la récupération juste-à-temps sont les trois tactiques qui gardent les agents longs cohérents. Organiser le contexte, c'est le même levier que réduire les coûts — moins de tokens, de meilleures réponses, une facture plus basse.

Voici une lentille autour de laquelle AILmanac est construit, et l'idée la plus utile que nous puissions vous transmettre sur le travail avec l'IA : Tous les faits sur l'IA ne se périment pas à la même vitesse. Vous ne devriez donc pas les traiter de la même manière. Le prix d'un modèle, le nom du « meilleur » modèle, le fonctionnement des transformers — ce sont tous des « faits », mais l'un change chaque semaine, l'autre chaque mois, et le dernier n'a pratiquement pas changé depuis des années. Si vous stockez les trois dans votre tête avec une confiance égale, vous vous tromperez avec assurance sur deux d'entre eux d'ici un mois. Un modèle que nous trouvons utile : attribuez à chaque fait une demi-vie de fraîcheur — une estimation grossière du temps qu'il faut avant qu'il ait 50 % de chances d'être périmé — puis décidez comment le gérer en fonction de cette demi-vie, et non en fonction de son importance ressentie.

Il n'y a que trois choses que vous pouvez faire d'un fait : Le mettre en cache — le garder en tête et agir dessus sans re-vérifier. Le re-vérifier — partir du principe qu'il a pu dériver ; le vérifier auprès d'une source avant de vous y fier. Lier, ne pas mémoriser — ne jamais stocker la valeur du tout ; stocker un pointeur vers l'endroit où vit la valeur à jour. L'erreur que presque tout le monde commet, c'est de mettre en cache des choses qui devraient être liées. On mémorise un prix, on le répète en réunion six mois plus tard, et on a tort. La demi-vie de fraîcheur vous indique quel geste adopter.
documents.s: Le geste fondamental : adapter la gestion à la demi-vie

documents.t: Un modèle que nous trouvons utile consiste à trier les faits sur l'IA en quatre niveaux de péremption. Les frontières sont floues à dessein — l'important, c'est le gradient, pas des seuils exacts. Niveau Demi-vie Exemples Que faire Volatil Heures–jours Prix exacts, limites de débit, état des files/de la capacité, libellés d'interface et noms de boutons en direct, « l'API est-elle opérationnelle en ce moment » Lier, ne pas mémoriser. Ne jamais citer de mémoire. Toujours récupérer la valeur à jour depuis la source officielle au moment où vous en avez besoin. Rapide Semaines Quel modèle est le « meilleur » ou le « par défaut » pour une tâche, paramètres recommandés, quelles fonctionnalités sont en préversion Re-vérifier avant de s'y fier. Vous pouvez retenir une hypothèse de travail ; vérifiez avant de miser quoi que ce soit dessus. Lent Mois Quelles fonctionnalités existent réellement, noms d'outils et de produits, grands paliers de capacité (« peut-il voir des images ? ») Mettre en cache, mais dater. Gardez-le en tête, mais attachez-y un « valable vers telle date » mental et re-vérifiez quand les enjeux sont élevés. Durable Années Comment les transformers prédisent les tokens, pourquoi les fenêtres de contexte comptent, les principes de prompting, l'échelle de confiance, ce cadre même Mettre en cache librement. Ce sont les fondations qui valent la peine d'être réellement apprises. Investir ici produit des intérêts composés.

Le piège, c'est la confusion de niveau — traiter un fait volatil comme s'il était durable. « Claude coûte X $ par million de tokens » ressemble à un fait solide, alors les gens le mettent en cache. Mais sa demi-vie se compte en jours, pas en années. La solution n'est pas de mémoriser plus fort ; c'est de le faire descendre d'un niveau dans la façon de le gérer : lier à la source au lieu de citer un chiffre. L'erreur inverse est plus rare mais réelle : re-googler les choses durables (« comment fonctionne un LLM ? ») à chaque fois au lieu de simplement les apprendre une bonne fois. Si la demi-vie d'un fait se mesure en années, arrêtez de la re-vérifier et intériorisez-la. Un test rapide quand vous vous surprenez à énoncer un fait sur l'IA : « Quelle est la demi-vie de ce que je viens de dire ? » Si la réponse honnête est « des jours », vous devriez pointer vers une source, pas vers votre mémoire.

La plupart des domaines présentent un mélange confortable de faits durables et volatils. L'IA est inhabituelle : une grande part des « faits » que les gens répètent appartiennent aux niveaux Volatil et Rapide — noms de modèles, prix, limites, ce qui est le meilleur cette semaine. Le ratio volatil/durable est élevé. C'est précisément pour cela que tant de conseils sur l'IA vieillissent mal, et pourquoi une habitude axée sur la fraîcheur rapporte davantage ici que dans des domaines qui bougent plus lentement. Cela explique aussi une règle contre-intuitive : plus une astuce paraît sûre d'elle au sujet d'un chiffre précis, plus vous devriez vous en méfier. Précision et fraîcheur sont souvent en tension. « Utilisez le modèle compétent le moins cher » est un conseil durable. « Utilisez le modèle X à Y $ » est une capture d'écran d'un instant.
documents.s: Pourquoi cela compte plus pour l'IA que pour presque tout le reste

documents.t: Ce n'est pas qu'une théorie que nous vous transmettons — c'est le système d'exploitation de tout le site. Les faits volatils ne sont jamais codés en dur dans la prose. Les prix, les limites et les noms de modèles actuels vivent à un seul endroit — data/models.json, notre source unique de vérité — et sur la page Modèles et tarification, que nous maintenons vérifiée. Partout ailleurs, nous lions vers ces sources plutôt que de répéter un chiffre qui se périmerait. Chaque page volatile porte un tampon <VerifyNote> indiquant quand un humain l'a vérifiée pour la dernière fois auprès de la source officielle, comme ceci : Dernière vérification : 2026-06-23. Most guides optimize the model and the prompt. But once an agent's work is too big to finish in one context window — a multi-day refactor, a research project, a migration across hundreds of files — the thing that decides whether it succeeds is rarely the model. It's the harness: the scaffolding around the model that carries state forward, checks that progress is real, and recovers when a step goes wrong. A useful definition: a harness encodes everything the model can't reliably do on its own. The model reasons and acts within a turn; the harness makes those turns add up to something across sessions. Dernière vérification : 2026-08-08. Framing and patterns here draw on Anthropic's engineering write-ups, primarily "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" and its companion "Effective context engineering for AI agents." Read those for the canonical, first-party version. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.

A context window is a hard ceiling. Most non-trivial projects can't be completed inside one. So a long-running agent doesn't run as one giant conversation — it runs as a sequence of bounded sessions, each starting roughly fresh. That creates the central problem: how does session N+1 know what session N did? Without an answer, the agent either re-discovers everything (slow, expensive, error-prone) or contradicts its earlier self. The harness's first job is to bridge that gap.

The bridge is built from two things the model doesn't have natively: Artifacts — durable outputs left in the world: committed code, a written plan, a progress log, updated tests. The next session reads them instead of re-deriving them. External memory — a deliberately curated store (files, a scratchpad, a task list) holding the high-signal state: what's done, what's next, what was decided and why. Before the window fills, the agent summarizes the completed phase into memory and lets the raw turn-by-turn history fall away. This is compaction — trading verbose history for a compressed, reloadable summary. The discipline is the same as context engineering: not "remember everything," but "carry forward the smallest set of high-signal tokens that lets the next session continue correctly."
documents.s: What the harness carries between sessions

documents.t: A pattern Anthropic describes for the Claude Agent SDK splits the job in two: An initializer runs once, on the first session: it sets up the environment — dependencies, config, a map of the codebase, the plan — so later sessions don't pay that cost repeatedly. A worker runs every session after: it makes one increment of progress and, crucially, leaves clear artifacts for the next worker before it stops. The insight is that "start the work" and "continue the work" are different jobs with different context needs. Conflating them wastes the window re-initializing every time.

A long-running agent compounds its own errors: a wrong assumption in session 2 becomes the foundation for sessions 3 through 30. The harness has to make progress checkable — tests it can run, a build it can break, a linter, an explicit "definition of done" — so the agent catches drift early instead of confidently building on sand. This is the capability–reliability gap in operational form: the model is capable of the step, but only a verification loop makes a sequence of steps reliable. Where you let the agent act without that check is exactly where you've placed it on the trust ladder.
documents.s: Verification is part of the harness, not an afterthought

documents.t: A practical checklist when work will outlast one window: Externalize state early. Decide now where progress lives — a PROGRESS.md, a task list, commits — not when the context is already full. Make sessions resumable. Each session should be able to start from artifacts alone. If it needs the previous chat to make sense, the harness is leaking state. Compact deliberately. Summarize finished phases into memory before the window forces a messy truncation. Build in a checkpoint. Give the agent a command that answers "is the work still correct?" — and have it run before declaring a step done. Plan for recovery. Assume a session will fail mid-step. The next one should detect the half-done state and continue, not duplicate or corrupt it. The takeaway: for short tasks, optimize the prompt. For work that spans sessions, optimize the harness — it's the part that turns a capable model into a dependable one.
