What you'll learn Understand the two-agent split (shopping vs merchant) and why Anthropic did NOT use an intent router or domain subagents Learn the staged-write guardrail: how no model tool call ever moves money or mutates the store — every write ends at a human-approved surface See the three runtime paths (Messages API, Agent SDK, Managed Agents) and how the SAME core code plugs into all three Steal three transferable patterns for any agent that touches a real business system: server-issued IDs, fenced third-party text, and prompt-vs-skill split On September 2, 2026 Anthropic published anthropics/commerce-agents — an Apache 2.0 reference blueprint for building shopping and merchant agents on Claude. It ships two working agents, four vertical examples (retail, travel, telecom, entertainment), and — crucially — a set of guardrail patterns implemented in code, not in prompts. Anthropic states the repo is a reference implementation they will not maintain as a product and does not accept outside contributions. The interesting thing is not that you can now build a shopping bot. The interesting thing is the shape: an unusually opinionated take on how an agent that touches real business systems should be structured. Everything below is transferable to any agent that has to write to a real backend — inventory, customer records, banking, ops tooling.

Anthropic ships one shopping agent (customer-facing) and one merchant agent (staff-facing), each with its own backend interface (StorefrontBackend and MerchantBackend) and its own set of skills. They deliberately did not build: an intent router that dispatches to sub-agents per-domain subagents (a "cart agent" + "returns agent" + "search agent") one monolithic agent that does both consumer and staff work Instead: one unified agent per audience, in a standard agent loop, with skills and tools. Their guidance in the anatomy of effective commerce agents post: "anything the agent needs on most turns generally goes in the system prompt" — so for a shopping agent, catalog search lives in the prompt because it's on nearly every turn. "The rest goes in skills." Customer care, personalization, returns — skills. This is a strong opinion. Intent routers and domain subagents are the default architecture in a lot of tutorials, and Anthropic is telling you: for a single audience with tightly coupled sessions, don't.
documents.s: The split: two agents, not one

documents.t: Pro tip The single most important line in the blueprint: 'No model tool call moves money or changes the business.' Every mutation goes through a server-controlled approval step. If you take one thing from the repo, take this. The blueprint enforces safety in code, not prompts. The mechanism has three parts: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 11. Server issues every ID the model is allowed to reference⌄ The server maintains a per-session record of every product ID, SKU, campaign ID, and price ID it has handed the model. Writes and renders will ONLY accept IDs from that record. If the model hallucinates a SKU, the harness refuses — no prompt engineering required. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Every write is staged, never applied⌄ Order placement, payments, refunds, price changes, and campaign launches all end in a server-generated draft with its own approval ID. The tool call returns the draft ID and a preview. Nothing is live yet. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Approval happens on a real human surface⌄ A staged change only succeeds when the approval ID is signed off through a real UI — a button in the operator's portal, a confirmation in the CLI. The agent cannot self-approve; the approval endpoint doesn't accept model-generated identity. ←PreviousNext→ The blueprint also handles two other classic footguns: Regulated content: for fees, disclosures, and price-shown-to-consumer, the model chooses which product to disclose; the words come from server-supplied approved copy. The model never writes disclosure text. Third-party text sanitization: any user-generated content (reviews, seller notes, messages) is wrapped in "fenced text" markers before it reaches the model, so it can't smuggle instructions into the prompt.

The blueprint places no orders and charges no cards. Checkout is rendered for the host application to complete. In Anthropic's words, this "keeps payment handling, fraud rules and credentials outside the agent." Visa, Mastercard, and Accenture are named partners on the announcement, but the payment step lives in your existing checkout or an agentic payments provider — never in the model's tool surface. This is another opinionated line: if it can lose money in one shot, the model doesn't touch it.

The repo splits every agent into a core package (types, backend interface, prompt, tool contracts) and separate runtime packages that adapt the core to different serving surfaces: Messages API — the reference loop CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from shopping_agent import ShoppingAgentConfig from shopping_agent_runtime import ShoppingAgent agent = ShoppingAgent( backend=your_backend, skills_dir=Path("shopping-agent/skills"), config=ShoppingAgentConfig(brand_name="Your Store"), ) async for event in agent.stream_turn(messages, session, state): # yields: text_delta | tool_call | ui | cart_update | turn_complete ... await agent.update_memory(messages, session) Agent SDK — with a local console CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ python shopping-agent/runtime-agent-sdk/main.py \ --once "a two-person tent under $250" python merchant-agent/runtime-agent-sdk/main.py # prints staged changes and waits for y/n approval Managed Agents (beta) — hosted CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ scripts/deploy_managed_agent.sh \ shopping-agent/managed-agents/shopping-agent # The manifest declares tools + a storefront MCP server; # Anthropic hosts the loop. The same core/ code runs under all three, which is the actual portable pattern: keep the agent's contract (tools, prompt, backend interface) separate from the serving harness. If you swap Messages API for Managed Agents six months from now, only the runtime package changes.

Long-term memory (preferences, past orders, service notes) is persisted in your existing databases, not in model context. Extraction happens asynchronously after the conversation ends — you don't pay latency to update memory on the hot path. On the next turn, the runtime hydrates relevant memory into the system prompt. This is worth internalizing even if you're not building commerce: shoving conversation summaries into context on every turn is a common performance mistake. The blueprint's shape — write async, read on turn-start — is the cheaper one.

examples/ includes end-to-end demos for four verticals, each with a different structural wrinkle you can copy: Retail — the base case. Standard catalog, cart, checkout. Travel — date-bound inventory (a flight seat expires), itinerary presentation with multi-leg comparison. Telecom — account context ("your current plan is X"), plan matrices, regulated fee disclosure. Entertainment — timed holds on tickets, waitlists, venue seat maps. If your product isn't commerce but has any of these traits (expiring inventory, regulated disclosure, timed holds), the matching vertical is worth reading before you design your own agent.
documents.s: The four verticals (and why they differ)

documents.t: Clone, install, run one vertical CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/anthropics/commerce-agents.git cd commerce-agents python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (cd examples && npm ci) python scripts/run_demo.py retail # API on :8000, storefront on :3000 The repo verifies with ruff check . && ruff format --check . && pytest && python scripts/check.py, and there's a python scripts/verify_all.py for the comprehensive pass.

Copier en Markdown Avancé Chaque grand laboratoire propose aujourd'hui un modèle capable de regarder un écran et de cliquer dessus. L'outil computer use d'Anthropic, l'outil computer d'OpenAI et l'outil computer_use de Google résolvent tous le même type de problème — prendre une capture d'écran, décider d'une action, l'exécuter, reprendre une capture — et tous les trois sont incompatibles entre eux au niveau du protocole, d'une manière qui ne saute pas aux yeux tant que les clics n'atterrissent pas 40 pixels à côté. Cette page est le guide au niveau du harnais, pas le classement. Le classement change tous les mois ; les modes de défaillance ci-dessous sont les mêmes depuis la toute première préversion. What you'll learn Comprendre la boucle d'agent commune aux trois fournisseurs — et les trois points où ils divergent Corriger le bug de coordonnées qui casse silencieusement la plupart des premières tentatives (Retina, réduction d'échelle et limites de taille d'image) Connaître la barrière de sécurité de chaque fournisseur, car elle fait partie du protocole et n'est pas un ajout facultatif Lire OSWorld honnêtement : ce que signifie réellement la référence humaine Choisir correctement l'effort de raisonnement — le réglage le moins cher n'est pas celui qu'on croit Dernière vérification : 2026-07-14. Les noms de modèles, les en-têtes beta, les limites de pixels et les scores de benchmark évoluent vite dans ce domaine, et chaque fournisseur qualifie encore sa surface computer-use de préversion ou de beta. Les mécaniques décrites ci-dessous sont durables ; revérifiez chaque chiffre, en-tête ou identifiant de modèle précis dans la documentation du fournisseur liée dans les Sources avant de passer en production. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.

Une fois la marque mise de côté, les trois sont la même machine à états : Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Envoyer la tâche accompagnée d'une capture d'écran⌄ Le modèle reçoit votre instruction et une image de l'écran courant. Certains fournisseurs veulent aussi l'URL courante ou un bref historique des actions récentes. ←PreviousNext→ 2Le modèle renvoie une action, pas un résultat⌄ Clique en (x, y). Tape ceci. Fais défiler ici. C'est une demande adressée à votre code — le modèle ne peut pas toucher la machine lui-même. ←PreviousNext→ 3Votre harnais l'exécute⌄ Cette partie vous appartient. Anthropic le dit clairement : votre application doit exécuter l'outil ; Claude ne peut pas l'exécuter directement. C'est vous qui implémentez la capture d'écran, la souris et le clavier. ←PreviousNext→ 4Reprendre une capture et la renvoyer⌄ Le nouvel écran repart comme résultat d'outil. Le modèle voit la conséquence de sa propre action — c'est tout le signal de retour dont il dispose. ←PreviousNext→ 5Répéter jusqu'à ce qu'aucune action ne revienne⌄ La terminaison, c'est l'absence de nouvelle demande d'action, pas un indicateur « terminé ». Votre boucle a besoin de son propre plafond d'étapes et d'une détection de blocage. ←PreviousNext→ La conséquence qu'on néglige : la seule perception du monde qu'a le modèle est l'image que vous lui envoyez. Chaque défaillance ci-dessous est en réalité une défaillance de cette image, ou de l'espace de coordonnées qu'elle implique.

La divergence n'est pas « lequel est le plus intelligent ». C'est le contrat. Anthropic (Claude) OpenAI (GPT) Google (Gemini) Espace d'actions Primitives brutes du bureau : screenshot, left_click, type, key, scroll, drag, hold_key, wait, plus zoom sur la version la plus récente de l'outil Actions d'interface structurées : click, double_click, scroll, type, keypress, drag, move, wait, screenshot Actions sémantiques : pas seulement click/type mais navigate, go_back, go_forward, open_app, long_press — les concepts du navigateur et du mobile sont de première classe Coordonnées Vous envoyez les dimensions en pixels ; le modèle renvoie des coordonnées en pixels bruts dans cet espace Même contrat de pixels, avec des tailles de bureau recommandées Idem, avec un champ intent expliquant le raisonnement derrière chaque action Plomberie de la boucle Blocs de résultat d'outil portant une image computer_call → computer_call_output associés par call_id ; previous_response_id porte l'historique pour que vous n'ayez pas à le renvoyer Appel de fonction → function_result avec une nouvelle capture d'écran Barrière de sécurité Des classificateurs d'injection s'exécutent automatiquement sur les captures d'écran pending_safety_checks que vous devez explicitement acquitter safety_decision avec des catégories de politique Terrain de prédilection Contrôle général du bureau / au niveau de l'OS Bureau et navigateur, plus un chemin d'exécution de code Navigateur d'abord ; fort sur mobile ; explicitement non optimisé pour le contrôle d'un OS de bureau Cette dernière ligne Anthropic/Google est celle qui décide de l'architecture. L'espace d'actions de Google est sémantique — go_back est un concept que le modèle peut nommer. Celui d'Anthropic est mécanique — revenir en arrière signifie que le modèle doit trouver et cliquer le bouton retour, ou presser la bonne combinaison de touches. Les actions sémantiques sont plus fiables dans un navigateur et inutiles en dehors. Les primitives mécaniques fonctionnent partout et échouent plus souvent. Donc : porter un agent computer-use d'un fournisseur à un autre n'est pas un simple changement de modèle. C'est réécrire l'exécuteur d'actions du harnais. Budgétisez en conséquence. (Même leçon que dans Comparatif des CLI d'agents de codage : c'est au harnais, pas au modèle, que vous êtes réellement marié.)

C'est l'élément à plus forte valeur de cette page, parce que presque tout le monde le rencontre et que le symptôme ressemble à « le modèle est mauvais pour cliquer ». Il n'est pas mauvais pour cliquer. Votre image et votre espace de coordonnées sont en désaccord. Trois causes indépendantes, qui se cumulent :
documents.s: Le bug de coordonnées qui dévore votre première semaine

documents.t: Les écrans Retina de macOS capturent des captures d'écran avec un ratio de pixels de l'appareil de 2 — l'image fait deux fois la résolution des coordonnées logiques de l'écran. Envoyez-la telle quelle et le modèle raisonne sur une image de 2880 de large tandis que votre exécuteur de clics pense en points logiques de 1440 de large. Chaque clic atterrit à peu près à la moitié de la position visée, de manière constante, dans une seule direction. Correctif : réduire l'échelle par 2 avant l'envoi, ou diviser par deux les coordonnées renvoyées par le modèle. Pas les deux.

Les modèles ont des limites de taille d'image — et elles diffèrent entre modèles d'un même laboratoire. Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 et Opus 4.7 acceptent jusqu'à 2576 pixels sur le côté long ; les modèles Claude antérieurs acceptent 1568 pixels et environ 1,15 mégapixel au total. Voici le piège : si vous envoyez quelque chose de plus grand, l'API en réduit l'échelle pour vous au lieu de renvoyer une erreur. Le modèle renvoie alors des coordonnées dans l'espace de l'image que lui a vue — et vous n'avez jamais connu le facteur d'échelle, puisque le redimensionnement a eu lieu côté serveur. Seules les images vraiment énormes (au-delà d'environ 8 000 px de côté) sont rejetées d'emblée avec une erreur de validation. Ainsi, c'est le comportement « serviable » qui est le bug. Redimensionnez toujours côté client, définissez display_width_px/display_height_px aux dimensions que vous avez réellement envoyées, et remettez vous-même à l'échelle les coordonnées renvoyées.
documents.s: 2. L'API réduit silencieusement l'échelle des images trop grandes

documents.t: Avec l'outil d'OpenAI, les captures d'écran doivent utiliser detail: "original" — "high" comme "low" dégradent la précision des clics pour cette tâche précisément. Et si vous redimensionnez sans préserver le rapport d'aspect, les clics atterrissent dans la bonne zone et ratent la cible. Mise à l'échelle des coordonnées — la forme du correctif CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Before sending: shrink to fit the model's image limit, remember the factor. LONG_EDGE_LIMIT = 2576 # check YOUR model's limit; older Claude models: 1568 scale = min(1.0, LONG_EDGE_LIMIT / max(width, height)) sent_w, sent_h = round(width * scale), round(height * scale) # -> send the resized image, and declare display_width_px=sent_w, display_height_px=sent_h # After the model replies: map its coordinates back to the real screen. real_x, real_y = model_x / scale, model_y / scale # On a Retina capture you did NOT pre-downscale, divide by the device pixel ratio too.
documents.s: 3. Réglages de détail et rapport d'aspect

documents.t: Symptôme Presque certainement Clics systématiquement décalés dans une direction Vos display_width_px/display_height_px déclarés ne correspondent pas à l'image réellement envoyée Les clics atterrissent dans la bonne zone mais ratent les petites cibles Détail perdu à la réduction d'échelle, ou rapport d'aspect déformé au redimensionnement Précision mauvaise partout Résolution trop basse — essayez 1280x720 comme plancher Le modèle lit mal les petits textes (titres d'onglet, noms de fichiers, numéros de ligne) Il a besoin de zoomer, et vous ne l'avez pas activé Recommandations de résolution, données par les fournisseurs eux-mêmes : Anthropic suggère 1024x768 ou 1280x720 pour un bureau généraliste, 1280x800 ou 1366x768 pour les applications web, et déconseille explicitement de dépasser 1920x1080. OpenAI recommande 1440x900 ou 1600x900. Plus grand n'est pas mieux — vous payez des tokens pour des pixels, puis vous jetez le détail à la réduction d'échelle.

La toute dernière version de l'outil computer de Claude (computer_20251124) ajoute une action zoom, désactivée par défaut — il faut définir enable_zoom: true. Une fois activée, Claude zoome sur une région lorsqu'il doit lire du petit texte illisible à la résolution de base de la capture : noms de fichiers de la barre latérale, titres d'onglet, texte de la barre d'état, numéros de ligne, libellés de boutons. Note opérationnelle non évidente : si Claude ne zoome pas alors que vous vous y attendez, le correctif consiste généralement à poser la question sur une région ou un élément précis plutôt que sur l'écran dans son ensemble.
documents.s: La soupape de secours du zoom

documents.t: Ne les traitez pas comme un rajout. Dans les trois API, le mécanisme de sécurité modifie la forme de votre boucle. Anthropic a entraîné le modèle à résister à l'injection de prompt et exécute automatiquement des classificateurs sur vos prompts dès que les outils computer-use sont en jeu. Quand un classificateur repère une injection probable dans une capture d'écran, il oriente le modèle vers une demande de confirmation à l'utilisateur avant l'action suivante. C'est excellent avec un humain présent et carrément inadapté pour un pipeline non surveillé — d'où l'existence d'une désactivation, conditionnée à une prise de contact avec le support. OpenAI expose des pending_safety_checks que votre code doit explicitement acquitter (acknowledged_safety_checks) avant que la boucle ne se poursuive. La barrière est entre vos mains, et la contourner est une décision que vous prenez dans le code. Google renvoie une safety_decision — autorisée, require_confirmation, ou bloquée — pilotée par des catégories de politique dont FINANCIAL_TRANSACTIONS, COMMUNICATION_TOOL, ACCOUNT_CREATION, SENSITIVE_DATA_MODIFICATION et LEGAL_TERMS_AND_AGREEMENTS. Le filtrage des injections de prompt dans les captures d'écran est disponible en option à activer. La menace est réelle et précise : une capture d'écran est une entrée non fiable. Du texte affiché sur une page web, dans une image, dans un PDF ouvert par l'agent — tout cela atteint le modèle par le même canal que vos instructions. La documentation d'Anthropic note elle-même que Claude suivra, dans certaines circonstances, des instructions trouvées dans le contenu même lorsqu'elles entrent en conflit avec les vôtres. Les mesures d'atténuation de chaque fournisseur convergent vers les trois mêmes règles : isolez l'environnement, gardez un humain sur les actions à fort impact, et considérez tout ce qui est à l'écran comme hostile. Si l'agent doit se connecter, ce risque grimpe fortement — des identifiants plus du contenu injectable, c'est la pire combinaison dans ce domaine. Voir Sécuriser les agents locaux et hybrides et Injection de prompt pour le manuel défensif.
documents.s: Les barrières de sécurité font partie du protocole

documents.t: OSWorld est l'étalon partagé, et c'en est un bon parce qu'il est difficile à truquer : il place un agent dans un vrai OS avec de vraies applications, et note avec une vérification basée sur l'exécution — un script contrôle si le fichier a réellement été enregistré, pas si l'agent affirme l'avoir fait. Le benchmark couvre 369 tâches (361 dans le jeu d'évaluation standard, puisqu'une poignée de tâches Google Drive nécessitent une configuration manuelle) et fournit 134 fonctions d'évaluation basées sur l'exécution. OSWorld-Verified en est la révision nettoyée, avec les exemples cassés signalés par la communauté corrigés et le temps d'évaluation ramené à environ une heure sur AWS. Deux chiffres qu'il faut tenir ensemble : La référence humaine est d'environ 72,4 %. Pas 100 %. Ces tâches sont réellement tatillonnes, et les humains s'y trompent aussi. Au lancement d'OSWorld, le meilleur modèle obtenait 12,24 %. Les agents de pointe rapportent aujourd'hui des scores dans les 70 % et au-delà — ce qui signifie que le titre « les agents ont atteint le niveau humain sur l'usage de l'ordinateur » est arithmétiquement défendable et pratiquement trompeur. Un score de benchmark est un résultat modèle + harnais + échafaudage, exactement comme un benchmark de codage (voir L'écart capacité–fiabilité). Votre harnais n'est pas le leur. Et un taux de réussite de 75 % sur des tâches isolées se compose brutalement : un flux de huit étapes où chaque étape est fiable à 95 % réussit environ 66 % du temps. Traitez OSWorld comme la preuve que la capacité existe, et votre propre jeu d'évaluation comme la seule preuve que votre produit fonctionne.

Pour le computer use de Claude en particulier, le benchmarking interne d'Anthropic donne des recommandations qui inversent l'intuition habituelle : Opus 4.7 : effort high par défaut ; descendez à low pour les charges à fort débit ou sensibles au coût. Sonnet 4.6 et Opus 4.6 : medium offre le meilleur rapport précision/coût. Évitez max — sur les tâches d'interface, il ajoute du coût en tokens sans améliorer la précision. Le contre-intuitif : sur ces modèles, l'effort low consomme moins de tokens de sortie que la désactivation complète du raisonnement. Un peu de réflexion évite les erreurs, et les erreurs vous coûtent des reprises — et les reprises coûtent bien plus de tokens que la réflexion. Donc « couper la réflexion pour économiser » est, pour le computer use, souvent faux. Le moins cher, c'est un peu de réflexion. Une dernière subtilité de sélection de modèle : la précision mécanique du clic n'est pas le même axe que l'intelligence. Sonnet 4.6 est mécaniquement plus précis au clic qu'Opus 4.6, et plus robuste quand les captures d'écran ont été fortement réduites. Opus 4.7 resserre cet écart et relève la limite de pixels, si bien qu'il nécessite moins de réduction d'échelle au départ.
documents.s: Le résultat sur l'effort de raisonnement auquel personne ne s'attend

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Bac à sable d'abord, toujours⌄ Un conteneur ou une VM sans rien de précieux dedans. Chaque fournisseur le dit et tous le pensent vraiment : l'agent finira par cliquer quelque chose que vous n'aviez pas prévu. ←PreviousNext→ 2Figer l'espace de coordonnées⌄ Capturez, redimensionnez côté client à la limite de votre modèle, déclarez les dimensions exactes envoyées, et conservez le facteur d'échelle. Écrivez cela une fois et n'y pensez plus jamais. ←PreviousNext→ 3Plafonner la boucle⌄ La terminaison, c'est « aucune action supplémentaire renvoyée » — ce qui ne se produit jamais si l'agent est coincé dans une fenêtre modale qu'il ne sait pas fermer. Ajoutez un budget d'étapes maximal et un détecteur de blocage (N captures d'écran identiques d'affilée). ←PreviousNext→ 4Décider explicitement de votre politique de barrière de sécurité⌄ Humain dans la boucle, ou fonctionnement non surveillé avec désactivation et rayon d'impact réduit. Ne découvrez pas cela par accident quand une demande de confirmation bloquera votre tâche cron. ←PreviousNext→ 5Construire une évaluation de dix tâches avant de construire la deuxième fonctionnalité⌄ Vérifiée par l'exécution, comme le fait OSWorld : contrôlez que le monde a changé, pas que l'agent l'a dit. C'est le seul chiffre sur votre système qui ait un sens. ←PreviousNext→ 6Préférer l'API aux pixels quand c'est possible⌄ L'agent computer-use le plus fiable est celui qui n'a pas besoin d'utiliser l'ordinateur. Si la cible a une API, un serveur MCP ou une CLI, ce chemin est plus rapide, moins cher et infiniment plus fiable. Les écrans sont le repli, pas l'objectif. ←PreviousNext→ Cette dernière étape est celle qui est stratégique. Le computer use est l'adaptateur universel pour les logiciels sans API — applications de bureau héritées, portails de fournisseurs, tout ce qui se cache derrière une connexion sans histoire d'intégration. C'est un magnifique bricolage, et cela reste un bricolage. Tournez-vous d'abord vers MCP et les vrais outils. Check yourself 0/5

Copier en Markdown Avancé At 09:08 UTC on 20 October 2026, a link titled "DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models" hit Hacker News and settled at 2,251 points and 856 comments — the biggest AI story on the site that week. The repository, deepseek-ai/DeepInfer, had been created four days earlier and collected 16,337 stars and 1,620 forks by the following morning. Apache 2.0. Written in Python. The framing everywhere was "DeepSeek open-sources the engine that runs DeepSeek." That framing is true and almost useless. The 856-comment thread is a near-perfect demonstration of the gap: it is an extended argument about whether inference is profitable for frontier labs, and contains essentially no discussion of what the code does. Nobody in it reports trying to run it. So this page does the unglamorous part. Four things in DeepInfer's own documentation materially change what you should conclude from the release, and none of them made the coverage: It is a vLLM fork, by its own acknowledgments — not a clean-room engine. "NVIDIA SM100" rules out every H100 and every consumer card. Most readers cannot run this at all. Its headline decode throughput is computed under full-acceptance accounting — it counts speculative draft tokens regardless of the true acceptance rate. Its most durable contribution, batch-invariant inference, is turned on by a flag that turns off DeepInfer's own speculative decoder. Speed and reproducibility are an either/or here. What you'll learn Describe accurately what DeepInfer ships and what it explicitly withholds — a KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation and DP load balancing are all absent, so this is an engine, not a server Decode the hardware line: SM100 means datacenter Blackwell, which excludes SM90 (H100/H200) and SM120 (RTX 50-series), and pair that with ~763 GB of FP8 weights to size a real deployment Explain why temperature 0 was never deterministic — and why the popular 'GPUs plus floating point are random' explanation is wrong Apply DeepInfer's deterministic-sampling recipe, and recognise the cost: the same flag disables the variable-length MTP path that DSpark rides on Read the published prefill/decode numbers correctly, including full-acceptance accounting, per-GPU normalisation, and why the profiler traces must never be used to derive steps-per-second Set the two configuration values that corrupt output or waste capacity when you get them wrong: SWA replay keep-tokens and EPLB redundant experts Dernière vérification : 2026-10-21. Star counts, the supported-model list (today: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash only), the pinned dependency versions and the environment-variable names here were read from the repository on 21 October 2026, four days after it was created. A four-day-old repo with 172 open issues and no tagged release will move fast — re-read the README and examples/README.md before you commit a deployment to any of it. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.
documents.s: DeepInfer: DeepSeek's Own Inference Engine, Read Honestly

documents.t: DeepInfer is the offline inference path of DeepSeek's production stack, extracted and published. It runs exactly one model family — DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash — on two hardware targets, with DeepSeek's own kernel libraries wired in: FlashMLA for multi-head latent attention, DeepGEMM for matrix multiply, DeepEP for expert-parallel communication, DeepSelect for sparse-attention and sampler top-k, and TileKernels plus in-tree TileLang kernels for the rest. Those five repos are not new — FlashMLA, DeepGEMM and DeepEP all date to February 2025 and carry 13.1k, 9.1k and 10.3k stars respectively; DeepSelect is from September 2026 and has 510. DeepInfer is the thing that was always missing: the scheduler and runtime that assembles them.
documents.s: What it is, in one paragraph

documents.t: Straight from the acknowledgments: DeepInfer "was originally built primarily on vLLM, with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM." That is worth sitting with. The dominant reading of this release was a frontier lab rejected the open-source serving stack and built its own. The opposite is closer to true: DeepSeek took vLLM, specialised it hard for one architecture on one class of accelerator, and gave the result back under the same permissive terms. If you already run vLLM, DeepInfer is a statement about what a vLLM derivative looks like when you delete all generality — not a competitor you must evaluate.

The README has a section most summaries skipped, titled "Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release)": a KV cache system VE/prefill/decode disaggregation (DeepSeek notes most of the engine-side functionality is implemented, but the orchestration is not) load balancing across data-parallel replicas, for both prefill and decode There is no OpenAI-compatible HTTP server here to point your client at. Every example is python examples/offline_inference.py. If your mental model was "swap vLLM out, swap DeepInfer in, same endpoint" — three of the hardest pieces of a serving platform are the ones you would be writing yourself. Watch out "Offline inference" is doing real work in that sentence. DeepInfer is a batch engine with the serving layer removed, which is exactly the shape you want for evals and for RL rollouts — and exactly the wrong shape for a production API without months of platform work.

The README lists two targets: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs. One line, and it quietly excludes almost everyone. SM100 is CUDA compute capability 10.0 — datacenter Blackwell, the B100/B200 class. It is not: Your hardware Arch Listed? H100 / H200 SM90 (Hopper) No RTX 5090 / 50-series SM120 (consumer Blackwell, cc 12.0) No B200 / B100 SM100 Yes Ascend 950 CANN 9.2 Yes And the two Blackwells are not interchangeable: there is no binary compatibility between sm_100 and sm_120, because datacenter Blackwell kernels use the tcgen05 instruction and TMEM — dedicated tensor memory that consumer Blackwell does not have at all. A kernel written for SM100 does not "run slower" on an RTX 5090; it does not run. The pinned dependency list says the same thing in a different dialect. requirements-nvidia.txt is three lines: torch==2.13.0+cu132, flash-attn-4==4.0.0b34, and the dev requirements — and build.sh then force-reinstalls nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.32.3 over whatever came with Torch. A beta FlashAttention-4 build, CUDA 13.2, and a hand-patched NCCL. This is a stack pinned to the exact machines in DeepSeek's own racks.

DeepInfer's default checkpoint is deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 — MIT-licensed, FP8, published 17 October 2026, spread over 48 safetensors shards. Hugging Face reports roughly 763 billion parameters for it. At FP8 that is on the order of 763 GB of weights before any KV cache, which is why the examples are written as --ep 8 and the decode benchmark runs on 64 GPUs. Eight 80 GB cards (640 GB) cannot hold it. You are looking at eight B200-class GPUs as a floor, inside a single scale-up domain, plus the three platform components DeepSeek didn't ship. Pro tip This is the practical answer to "should I switch?" for 99% of readers: you can't, and that's fine. The transferable value of this release is the three ideas below, each of which applies to the engine you actually run. If you want DeepSeek V4.1-Flash on hardware you own, the serving paths in our V4.1-Flash field guide (vLLM, SGLang, hosted API) still apply — and the -1017 checkpoint is a later revision than the September launch weights, so re-check its card rather than assuming parity.

This is the part of DeepInfer worth your attention even if you never run it. Set temperature=0, send the same prompt twice, get two different answers. Everyone has seen it. The explanation you have probably read — including in our own sampling-controls lesson, which this page sharpens — is "batching and floating-point non-determinism on the server side." That is the right neighbourhood and the wrong mechanism, and the distinction is what makes the bug fixable.
documents.s: Batch invariance: why temperature 0 was never deterministic

documents.t: "GPUs are parallel and floating-point addition isn't associative, so results wobble" implies the wobble is inherent. It isn't. Run the identical matrix multiplication on the identical data on the identical GPU as many times as you like and you get bitwise identical results every time. The kernel is deterministic. Concurrency is not the culprit.
documents.s: The wrong half of the explanation

documents.t: The culprit is batch invariance — or rather its absence. A GPU kernel picks its reduction strategy based on the shape of the work it's given. Multiply a single row (batch of 1) and the accumulation happens in one order; multiply that same row as part of a 32-row batch and the kernel splits the reduction differently, so the floating-point additions land in a different order, so the result differs in the last bits. Each run is deterministic. The shape is not. Then comes the part that makes it feel haunted: your batch size is decided by other people's traffic. A shared inference server batches your request with whatever else arrived in the same window. You changed nothing; the load did; your numerics moved. The forward pass is deterministic and your experience of it is not. In transformers, three reduction-based operations need fixing: RMSNorm, matrix multiply, and attention. The recipe is to keep each reduction inside one core where possible, refuse split reductions whose shape depends on batch size, and use a single kernel configuration even when that leaves performance on the table.

Thinking Machines Lab measured this on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507: the same prompt ("Tell me about Richard Feynman"), temperature 0, 1,000 tokens, 1,000 runs. Result: 80 unique completions. The most frequent appeared 78 times. And the shape of the divergence is the instructive bit — all 1,000 completions are identical for the first 102 tokens, then split at token 103, where 992 runs say "Queens, New York" and 8 say "New York City." That is why equality assertions in LLM test suites are so treacherous. A short smoke test passes a thousand times and tells you nothing; the divergence was waiting at token 103. Fixing it is not free. On Qwen-8B over 1,000 sequences, Thinking Machines measured vLLM's default at 26 s, a naive deterministic build at 55 s, and 42 s once the attention kernel was improved — so roughly 1.6× slower for bitwise reproducibility. Dernière vérification : 2026-10-21. The 80-completions result, the token-103 divergence and the 26 s / 55 s / 42 s figures are Thinking Machines Lab's measurements on their hardware and kernels, not DeepInfer's. DeepSeek publishes no comparable before/after cost for its own batch-invariant path. Treat ~1.6× as the order of magnitude to budget for, not a number to quote about DeepInfer. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.
documents.s: The number that should bother you

documents.t: Four reasons, in rough order of how much money they represent: On-policy RL stops being a lie. If your sampler and your trainer compute different numerics, your "on-policy" reinforcement learning is quietly off-policy. Thinking Machines showed that without deterministic inference you need off-policy correction to avoid reward collapse; with bitwise-identical results you get true on-policy RL and zero KL divergence between the sampling and training policies. For anyone doing RL on a large model, this is the headline, not a footnote. Regression tests can assert equality. DeepInfer leans on this hard: tests/models/offline_decode_ppl.json stores per-platform perplexity baselines that are compared exactly, sample by sample. That test design is only possible on a deterministic engine. Debugging an agent run becomes tractable. A failure you can replay bit-for-bit is a bug; one you can't is a ghost story. Audit and compliance. "Same input, same output, provably" is a requirement in some regulated settings and an impossibility without this.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Turn on batch invariance⌄ Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1. This holds each token's result bitwise identical regardless of what else shares its batch. NVIDIA only — the Ascend path does not offer it. ←PreviousNext→ 2Turn off the variable-length MTP path⌄ Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0. This is the same flag you set to 1 to enable DSpark speculative decoding, so by DeepSeek's own documentation the two features are mutually exclusive. ←PreviousNext→ 3Pin the sampler seed per sequence⌄ Pass a fixed seq_seed in SamplingParams. Identical input tokens plus identical sampling parameters then produce identical outputs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Decide which you actually need, per workload⌄ Determinism for evals, regression baselines and RL rollouts; DSpark for throughput on everything else. Running one cluster in each mode is a legitimate design, and cheaper than pretending one config serves both. ←PreviousNext→ DeepInfer: deterministic sampling (environment) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Deterministic sampling — NVIDIA only. # Note that MTP_VARLEN=0 is the same switch that disables DSpark, # so this configuration is deliberately the slow one. export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia export DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 export DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 # ...and pass a fixed seq_seed in SamplingParams, e.g. # SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, seq_seed=42) python examples/offline_inference.py --ep 8 DeepInfer: DSpark speculative decoding (the other mode) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Throughput mode: draft tokens plus confidence-scheduled verification. # DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE sets the maximum draft length (default 5). export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia export DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1 export DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE=5 # Explicitly disable speculative decoding instead: # export DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE=0 python examples/benchmark.py The second mode is where DeepInfer's cleverest idea lives. Plain speculative decoding drafts n tokens and verifies them all. Confidence-scheduled verification uses the model's own confidence estimates to decide how much verification budget to spend — cheap where the draft is obviously right, expensive where it isn't. That is a scheduling idea, not a kernel idea, and it transfers to any engine with a draft path.

DeepSeek publishes two Pareto curves — prefill throughput vs latency, decode throughput vs per-user speed — rather than a headline tokens-per-second figure. That restraint is admirable and it means there is no single number to quote. It also means the methodology, documented in examples/README.md, is where the truth lives. Three things in it change how you read the charts.

This is the big one. The published decode throughput is computed as: decode_throughput = avg_SPS × decode_num_requests × (1 + nextn) / cp and the documentation states plainly that this is "under the full-acceptance accounting — 1 + nextn tokens per request per step, regardless of the true acceptance rate." nextn defaults to 5. So each request is credited with 6 tokens per decode step whether the speculative decoder's 5 drafts survived verification or not. With the default 64 requests, "the 64 requests of one decode step account for 384 tokens in total" — 64 × 6. Real acceptance rates for multi-token prediction are well under 100%. So the decode throughput on that chart is an upper bound that no real workload reaches, and the gap between the chart and your reality is exactly your rejection rate. Nothing here is dishonest — it is written down in the repo — but it is not what a reader glancing at a Pareto curve assumes, and nobody in 856 Hacker News comments mentioned it.
documents.s: 1. Decode throughput assumes every draft token was accepted

documents.t: Prefill was measured on 4 SM100 GPUs, decode on 64, "each within one scale-up domain" — i.e. inside a single NVLink fabric, not across an Ethernet cluster. Both throughput figures are then divided by the device count to give tokens/s/GPU. Per-GPU normalisation is the right way to publish this, and it is also the easiest thing in the world to misread. A per-GPU decode number obtained with 64 GPUs sharing one fabric does not survive being multiplied back up on your 8-GPU node, because the expert-parallel communication pattern that made it possible was the fabric.
documents.s: 2. The numbers are per-GPU, at a scale you don't have

documents.t: A detail I have not seen anywhere else, and a genuinely useful warning for anyone profiling their own engine. From the docs: step times inside a PROFILE=1 trace include profiler overhead of "up to nearly 50% inflation at bsz=1", and even after the profiler exits there is a residual slowdown of ~7–11% — which is why no measurement is allowed to be scheduled after the profiler section. The explicit instruction is to use traces for inspecting kernel composition and never to derive steps-per-second. The harness goes further than most: it drops any measurement interval that collides with a MoE load-balancer statistics flush (an expert-parallel all_gather with a dozen milliseconds of jitter), and it runs the measurement window twice — once with logging on to capture load-balancer values, once silently for the actual numbers. Pro tip Steal the two-stage eval design regardless of engine. DeepInfer's eval harness separates generation from scoring: generation writes raw outputs to disk, scoring reads them back. You can re-judge with a different grader without paying for inference again — and on a deterministic engine you can prove the outputs didn't move.
documents.s: 3. The profiler traces are not throughput data

documents.t: Worth knowing before you cite any accuracy number from this repo. It covers three benchmarks, all reported as Pass@1: AIME 2026 (30 tasks × 32 samples, mean accuracy), HLE (2,500 questions — 2,158 text and 342 image — single sample), and GPQA Diamond (198 tasks × 8 samples). The scripts deliberately do not download the datasets; you must fetch each one yourself and convert it to JSONL, and HLE is gated on Hugging Face. A benchmark harness that refuses to auto-download its own test sets is a small sign of seriousness about contamination.
documents.s: What the eval harness actually measures

documents.t: SWA bounded replay. DeepInfer reduces decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix of context, configured with DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for V4.1's defaults. The constraint is the interesting part: the retained suffix must cover the sliding-window-attention window plus the maximum backtracking length. That oddly specific 140 is not a tuning preference, it is a floor derived from the architecture. Lower it to save memory and you are not trading quality for speed — you are truncating context the model still needs. EPLB redundant experts. Expert-parallel load balancing is configured through DEEPINFER_OVERRIDE_NUM_EXTRA_EXPERTS, default 32. This is only a lower bound: the engine rounds num_routed_experts + num_extra_experts up until it divides evenly by ep_size, rounding the backbone and DFlash separately. So the value you set is frequently not the value in effect — and the records written to disk and the plots use the rounded figure that actually took effect. If you are comparing two runs, compare the logged value, not your environment.

Ask what accounting a throughput number uses. "Tokens per second" with a speculative decoder in the loop is ambiguous until someone tells you whether rejected drafts are counted. Ask it of every engine, including the one you run. Stop asserting equality on LLM output unless you've earned determinism. Temperature 0 is near-deterministic, not deterministic, and the failure mode is a divergence a hundred tokens in that your smoke test never reaches. Either make the engine batch-invariant and assert bitwise, or test with evals and distributions. The middle ground is a flaky suite that teaches your team to ignore red. "Open-sourced the engine" rarely means "open-sourced the service." Read for the absences — cache system, disaggregation, load balancing. The gap between a published engine and a running service is where all the platform work lives, and the README that tells you honestly which pieces are missing is doing you a favour. Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways DeepInfer is a hard-specialised vLLM derivative for one model on datacenter Blackwell or Ascend 950 — not a general engine and not a drop-in server. Most readers cannot run it, and that is the honest answer to "should I switch?" It withholds the KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation and DP load balancing by design. Read releases for what is absent, not just what is announced. Batch invariance, not floating-point randomness, is why temperature 0 drifts: kernels pick reduction orders by batch shape, and co-tenant traffic picks your batch shape. 1,000 temperature-0 runs produced 80 unique completions, identical for 102 tokens and then not. Reproducibility costs roughly 1.6× throughput in published measurements, and in DeepInfer it also costs you DSpark — the enabling flag for one disables the other. Run separate configs for evals/RL and for serving. Full-acceptance accounting means the published decode throughput counts drafted tokens whether or not they were accepted. Ask every engine which accounting its tokens-per-second uses. DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 is an architectural floor, not a tuning dial; DEEPINFER_OVERRIDE_NUM_EXTRA_EXPERTS=32 is a lower bound the engine rounds up. Log the effective values before comparing runs.

documents.t: deepseek-ai/DeepInfer — Apache 2.0, created 16 October 2026, 16,337 stars / 1,620 forks / 172 open issues as of 21 October 2026. Copier en Markdown Avancé DeepSeek Harness — the command is dsh — is DeepSeek's open-source agent harness. It appeared on GitHub on 13 August 2026, carries 242,626 stars and 29,081 forks as of today, is MIT licensed and written in TypeScript. On 1 October 2026 DeepSeek added signed desktop installers, which is what put it back on the Hacker News front page. Its one-line pitch is the repository description: "Everything is a Plugin." That phrase is on the README of roughly every agent framework ever published, and it almost always means "we have a plugin folder." Here it means something much stronger and much weirder, stated plainly in docs/architecture.md: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop itself are plugins, "so each is replaceable from configuration." You can delete the agent loop from a YAML file and drop in your own without forking anything. That design has consequences — some excellent, some expensive. This page is about the ones you cannot read off the landing page. What you'll learn Understand what 'everything is a plugin' buys you here, and what Cordis — the framework underneath — actually guarantees Run your existing Claude Code hooks.json inside dsh, and know which subset survives the bridge Point dsh at Claude, GPT or a company gateway, and know why an OAuth subscription will not work Use PTC mode (run_code) deliberately instead of accidentally Read the three sandbox modes against the kernel primitive each one really uses Avoid the five configuration traps that cost an hour each Dernière vérification : 2026-10-03. Star counts, the npm version and the desktop installer matrix are perishable. The npm latest tag currently resolves to 0.2.0-rc.2 — a release candidate, not a stable release — and SAFETY.md describes the project as "experimental developer-preview software" that "has not undergone a security audit." The README warns of compatibility-breaking changes. Treat every file path, service key and config field below as true for the 0.2 line and re-check against the repository docs before you build on them. The architecture and safety claims here come from the repository's own documentation, not from secondary coverage. Vérifiez auprès de la source officielle.
documents.s: DeepSeek Harness: the agent where the agent loop itself is a plugin

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Start it⌄ `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` boots the web profile, prints a URL — `http://127.0.0.1:3080` — and opens your browser. No clone, no build. The directory you invoke it from becomes the default workspace root, but a fresh Web UI has no workspace selected until you add one, and the composer stays disabled until you do. ←PreviousNext→ 2Give it a model⌄ Settings → Models. The DeepSeek card takes an API key from platform.deepseek.com. Add a third-party provider and the shipped catalog offers provider ids including `anthropic`, `openai`, `moonshotai` (Kimi) and `zai` (GLM). Model changes apply on the next request — no restart. ←PreviousNext→ 3Understand where it put things⌄ Keys land in `$DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml`, write-only: the settings page gets a redacted descriptor back, never the secret, and your settings store only a credential reference. Everything else you change in the UI is written to `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml` — the same file you can hand-edit. ←PreviousNext→ 4Pick an entry mode⌄ `dsh web` is one of five shipped profiles. `dsh --profile headless "run the tests"` runs one persisted session, prints the final answer and exits — that is your CI entry point. `dsh --profile acp` serves automation clients over ACP stdio. `dsh --profile sdk` serves SDK clients over JSON-RPC stdio. The `desktop` name is reserved for the Electron app's own profile and the npm CLI refuses to boot it. ←PreviousNext→ 5Install plugins like npm packages⌄ `dsh plugin --profile web <pnpm args>` forwards straight to pnpm inside the profile directory. Plugins are ordinary packages in the profile's own `node_modules`. Community plugins are discoverable by the `dsh-plugin` GitHub topic. ←PreviousNext→

Underneath dsh is Cordis, a plugin framework vendored into the repository (vendor/) and described in an arXiv paper the project cites — A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability, arXiv:2608.25512, submitted 26 August 2026, from authors at Peking University and DeepSeek-AI. The paper's two ideas map directly onto how the harness behaves at runtime: Temporal composability — a component's side effects can be completely reversed when it is removed. In the harness this is ctx.effect(): prompt sections, tool schemas, model adapters, providers and listeners are all installed as reversible effects, so unloading a plugin unwinds its registrations in order rather than leaving orphans behind. Spatial composability — dependencies resolve reactively. A plugin names the services it needs via inject, and Cordis simply does not start it until those services exist. There is no boot sequence to maintain; load order is a consequence of declared requirements. A service claims a stable key on the shared context. The names are the architecture: Service key What owns it ctx.llm the LLM adapter registry — the model seam ctx.tools the tool registry and its scoped execution pipeline ctx.agentLoop the default agent-loop driver ctx.agents the live agent registry ctx.sessions the append-only SessionEvent log ctx.systemPrompt system-prompt assembly ctx.fs filesystem access ctx.subprocess subprocess execution ctx.sandbox subprocess confinement ctx.subagents subagent delegation ctx.ptcRuntime program execution for run_code ctx.credentials the credential seam The repository calls these capability seams, and splits every one into three roles: the package that declares the service, the packages that implement it, and the packages that consume it. ctx.sandbox is declared by packages/sandbox/sandbox, implemented by sandbox-local and sandbox-windows-acl, consumed by tool-bash and the PTC runtime. Replace the implementation and every consumer follows, with no consumer edits. Communication between plugins is typed events with five declared dispatch modes, and the mode is part of an event's public contract: Mode Awaited Order Returns a value emit no registration order no waterfall no registration order yes parallel yes all at once no serial yes registration order yes bail no registration order, stops at first bail yes waterfall is the interesting one: it is around-middleware. A listener gets (...args, next), calls next() to pass a possibly-wrapped result down the chain, or returns without calling next() to short-circuit. For single-decision events — "may this tool run?" — short-circuiting is the design: a policy listener that owns the decision returns without delegating, while a listener that merely annotates must delegate. If you have written a Claude Code hook that returns a deny decision, you already know this shape; the difference is that here it is the native extension mechanism rather than a shell-out. The agent loop runs turns (zero or more steps) and steps (one model request plus its tool calls), and the published extension sequence is agent/pre-step → agent/request → llm/stream → tools/* → step/end. Those are the hook points. You do not patch the loop; you listen to it.
documents.s: "Everything is a plugin" is a load-bearing claim

documents.t: This is the single most under-reported fact about dsh. packages/hooks ships three packages: hook-protocol (the shared engine), hooks-claude-code and hooks-codex. Point the Claude Code bridge at an existing hooks.json and your hooks run inside dsh when sessions start, prompts arrive, tools run and runs stop. The group README is explicit about what they can do: block prompts or tool calls with model-visible messages, add conversation context, or require the run to continue. The limit is equally explicit, and it is the thing to check before you plan a migration: each integration supports only the command-hook subset documented by its source tool. So your command-type hooks port. Anything that depends on Claude Code behaviour outside that subset does not. If you have a hooks layer you trust — see Claude Code hooks — this is a genuine "bring your guardrails with you" path, not a rewrite.
documents.s: 1. It will run your existing Claude Code hooks.json

documents.t: The provider list shipped in the installed catalog includes anthropic and openai by name. For anything not in the catalog — a relay, a company gateway, a self-hosted server — the custom-provider form asks for a Provider ID, a base URL, a credential and an API protocol, and offers exactly three: OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages. In cordis.patch.yml these are stored as openai-completions, openai-responses and anthropic-messages. Two consequences people trip over: A provider speaks one protocol. A gateway that serves both OpenAI and Anthropic shapes needs two provider entries, not one. OAuth sign-in is not supported. The providers guide states it directly, using Codex as its example: providers that sign in with OAuth "are not supported here yet." That means API-key billing, not a seat you already pay for. If you were hoping to drive dsh off an existing assistant subscription, budget for metered tokens instead — the arithmetic is in what AI costs across providers. There is also a model-discovery button that asks your endpoint which models it serves. Useful, with a caveat worth internalising: a built-in provider is always answered from the installed catalog even when its base URL points at a gateway. So if you want to see what a gateway really serves, you have to add it as a custom provider. Otherwise you are reading DeepSeek's shipped list back to yourself.
documents.s: 2. You can point it at Claude — but not with your subscription

documents.t: packages/ptc-runtime is the capability family behind what the tool registry presents to the model as run_code. The contract: the model writes one program that calls host-provided functions as ordinary async calls, and only the program's printed output and return value come back. Not the intermediate tool results. Not twenty round-trips. The specifics: The TypeScript backend runs each program in a fresh managed Node process under the resolved sandbox policy. Each run starts with no state from earlier programs. There is no implicit REPL session to lean on; carry state through files or the return value. Failures come back as results, not exceptions, so a caller can diagnose them or hand them to the model. An experimental Python backend exists, owning an fd-3 wire protocol between the Node host and a CPython subprocess, for when you genuinely need CPython. If this pattern is new to you, the clearest write-up of why it saves so much context is on Pi 1.0 and the codemode trick: tool results that never enter the transcript cannot inflate it. The same logic applies here. The difference is that in dsh the program runtime is a swappable seam (ctx.ptcRuntime) rather than a fixed sandbox choice.
documents.s: 3. run_code is codemode, and it is a first-class runtime

documents.t: The three modes will look familiar if you have configured Codex: Mode What a subprocess may do to files read-only read only workspace-write write only under the session workspace danger-full-access unrestricted What is more interesting is the backend table, because it tells you what is really enforcing the policy on your machine: Linux — bwrap, then Landlock as the fallback rung. macOS — Seatbelt. Windows — a restricted token, with sandbox-windows-acl as the write-restriction backend: confined children may write only in the workspace and a private temp directory. A denied call can retry through a user-approved one-time escalation, so the policy is a prompt-and-proceed boundary rather than a hard wall. And then the caveat, which the package README states itself and which you should quote to anyone who tells you this is "sandboxed": confinement is same-world only. It shares the host kernel and the host filesystem. Real isolation — containers, microVMs, remote executors — does not register here at all; it replaces whole capabilities instead. SAFETY.md is unusually candid for a 242k-star repository, and worth reading before a first run rather than after. It says the harness can execute model-generated code, load third-party plugins, reach the network and touch processes, credentials and files; that there is no inherent guarantee that sandboxing, approval prompts and permission controls will prevent damage to anything reachable; and that the software "must not be treated as secure or production-ready." Its own recommendations are the boring correct ones: disposable VMs or containers, backups of anything inside the project scope, and no sensitive credentials unless you accept the risk. The same reasoning applies to any harness you run locally — see securing local and hybrid agents and sandboxing and credential masking. There is also a small guard group worth knowing about: timeout-policy and repeat-tool-reminder — the latter being a nudge for the failure mode where a model calls the same tool in a loop.
documents.s: The sandbox: three modes, three kernel primitives, one honest caveat

documents.t: dsh persists sessions as a versioned JSONL file — session.vN.jsonl[.zstd] — with migration chains between versions, through a ctx.sessionPersistence seam whose shipped implementation is session-persistence-jsonl. Committed events include turn/start, step/start, user/message, assistant/message, tool/result and turn/end. The invariant behind it is the part to steal even if you never run dsh: "model-visible means logged." Every input the model saw must be reconstructable from the log. Live events exist separately, for driving UI in real time; they are explicitly not the record of truth. That single rule is what makes the surrounding packages possible: session-query-sqlite — query sessions out of SQLite instead of grepping JSONL. dsh-session-projection with ctx.sessionProjections — fold session state incrementally rather than replaying from zero. llm-replay plus token-meter ("replay token measurement") — replay a recorded session and measure its token cost, which is how you compare two prompt or model changes on identical inputs instead of on vibes. compaction-tool-result-pruner — described as model-free tool-result pruning, i.e. shrinking the transcript without paying a model to summarise it. Compare with Claude's own approach in context compaction. If you have ever tried to debug an agent run and discovered your logs recorded the rendered UI rather than the bytes the model received, you already know why this invariant is worth more than most features.
documents.s: The session log is the product

documents.t: dsh speaks MCP over both stdio and Streamable HTTP, using the official SDK for negotiation, discovery, validation and cancellation. The design choices are unusual enough to list: Servers are opt-in, one plugin entry per server. You configure one @deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client entry per server in the Cordis scope you want it visible in. There is deliberately no shared ctx.mcp service: the client is a connection plugin and a consumer of the tool registry. No configured server means no MCP tax. A caller with no visible configured server receives no MCP prompt text and no MCP tools, in native or PTC mode. Zero bytes, not "a small section." That matters more than it sounds — see the real cost of MCP tools. Public tool names include the server name, so identically-named tools from two servers stay distinct. A serverName must be unique inside its registration scope, but separate agent scopes may reuse it. Server instructions join the logged system prompt, bounded by the client's maxInstructionBytes. A verbose server cannot quietly annex your prompt — but note that this is also the channel through which a malicious server speaks to your model. That is the attack surface described in MCP tool poisoning and rug pulls. A failed tool-list refresh retains the previous tool generation rather than dropping your tools mid-session, and there is no product setting that forces a protocol revision — negotiation follows the SDK's supported revisions.
documents.s: MCP here is a per-server plugin, not a global registry

documents.t: A profile directory holds a package.json — out-of-tree plugin dependencies plus a dsh.profile manifest with an ordered bundles list — and a cordis.patch.yml, your own patch layer. The composed tree is built over an empty root in this order: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Each bundle's patch, in `dsh.profile.bundles` order⌄ Bundles resolve from the dsh installation first — `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base`, `dsh-web-app`, `dsh-headless`, `dsh-sdk-app`, `dsh-sdk-minimal`, `dsh-acp-app` — then from the profile's own `node_modules`, where pnpm installs out-of-tree plugins. `dsh-base` is the shared floor: model adapters, tools, persistence, sandbox policy. A bundle declares itself through a `dsh` field in its `package.json`. ←PreviousNext→ 2Then the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`⌄ `$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`. For a plain `dsh web` launch the profile is `web`. This is the file the Settings UI writes; you can edit it directly and the adapters re-read it on the next request. ←PreviousNext→ 3Then the home patch⌄ `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` — cross-profile overrides. ←PreviousNext→ 4Then `--patch` overlays⌄ Command-line overlays, applied last. `config/examples/` ships opt-in overlays for GitHub review webhooks, memory MCP servers and runtime Cordis tools; they are never part of a default profile. ←PreviousNext→ 5Inspect before you boot⌄ `--dump-default-config` and `--dump-config` print the composed tree without starting anything — the fastest way to answer "which layer set this?" ←PreviousNext→ With HMR enabled in YAML, dsh-hmr watches the profile manifest and both patch files and recomposes every layer through one serialized reload. Without it, changes apply on restart.
documents.s: Configuration: five layers, and the override that eats your providers

documents.t: A Cordis config override replaces the complete entry config. The providers guide spells this out: when you edit an existing override, you must preserve the other fields and other providers yourself. Patch one provider carelessly and you have deleted the rest. This is the single most expensive mistake available in cordis.patch.yml. A Provider ID is permanent. Requests, saved sessions, model defaults and credential references all key off it. Renaming means adding a new provider and deleting the old one. Display name, base URL, protocol, credential and model list stay editable. --dump-config-schema imports plugin code. Unlike the other dump flags, it loads the composed tree's declared plugin schemas to print JSON Schema — so pointing it at untrusted plugins executes their import-time code. The CLI reference has a dedicated safety note on this. Treat it like reviewing third-party code, not like --help. Plugin version compatibility is enforced, and the escape hatch is explicit. Installation and profile startup check declared DSH peer ranges against the runtime version from dsh --version; an incompatible plugin requires an acknowledged exact-version exemption (allow-version, revoke-version). Good hygiene, surprising the first time a plugin refuses to load. A session that has already sent a request keeps the model recorded in its own log. Changing the default model does not retroactively move a live session, and if a saved default names a deleted provider the composer blocks input until you pick another. Both are correct behaviour; both look like bugs at 1 a.m.
documents.s: Five gotchas that will cost you an hour

documents.t: Start the Web UI, then a headless one-shot run — no clone, no build CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Web UI on http://127.0.0.1:3080, workspace defaults to the invoking directory npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web # One persisted session, final answer to stdout, then exit — the CI shape npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile headless "summarize this repo and list its main packages" # Serve automation clients over ACP stdio (editor integrations) npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile acp # Inspect the composed config tree WITHOUT booting it npx @deepseek-ai/dsh --profile web --dump-config # Manage a profile's plugins (forwards to pnpm inside the profile directory) npx @deepseek-ai/dsh plugin --profile web add some-dsh-plugin Point dsh at a gateway that speaks Anthropic Messages — in $DSH_HOME/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # WARNING: a Cordis config override replaces the ENTIRE entry config. # Include every provider you want to keep, not just the new one. - id: llm-pi-ai config: providers: my-anthropic-gateway: apiKeyEnv: GATEWAY_API_KEY api: anthropic-messages # or openai-completions / openai-responses baseURL: https://gateway.example/v1 models: - id: some-text-model - id: some-vision-model input: [text, image] # omit to inherit the catalog's input types Bring your Claude Code guardrails across CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # The Claude Code hook bridge runs your existing command hooks inside dsh. # Only the command-hook subset documented by Claude Code is supported. # Hooks can: block a prompt or a tool call with a MODEL-VISIBLE message, # add conversation context, or require the run to continue. # # Check the bridge's own README for the current config field names before # wiring this up — the 0.2 line is a developer preview and they can move: # packages/hooks/hooks-claude-code/README.md # # Verify enforcement the same way you would in Claude Code: a hook that is # configured but never fires is worse than no hook, because you trust it.

If you are choosing a harness rather than studying one, the honest summary is: dsh is the most architecturally interesting open harness shipping right now and the least ready to be load-bearing. Its own safety file says so. The plugin model is genuinely stronger than its competitors' — ctx.agentLoop being replaceable is not a thing you can do in most harnesses at any price — and the hook bridges mean adopting it is not an all-or-nothing bet. Against that: a release-candidate latest tag, no security audit, promised breaking changes, and a provider story that assumes API keys. For a comparison across the field, see coding agent CLIs compared and local coding agents. For the models you would most plausibly drive it with, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Check yourself 0/7

SAFETY.md — what the harness can do to your machine, and the explicit "not secure or production-ready" statement. packages/sandbox/README.md — the three modes, the per-platform backends, escalation, and "same-world only". packages/hooks/README.md — the Claude Code and Codex hook bridges and the command-hook-subset limit. packages/ptc-runtime/README.md — the run_code contract, fresh-process execution, the experimental Python backend. docs/subsystems/mcp.md — per-server client plugins, scope rules, name namespacing, maxInstructionBytes, protocol negotiation. docs/user/guide/providers.md — provider ids, the three API protocols, OAuth limitation, credential storage, the override warning. apps/cli/README.md — entry modes, profile composition order, bundle names, dsh plugin, the dump flags, version exemptions.
